### Assistant (2026-11-01 08:08)

I've gone through the Blocksphere source and the runtime it's built on. Here's my read on your two symptoms and a plan for when you're back at your PC.

**Caveat:** I haven't built or run anything. Building needs your ROM, so everything below comes from reading the code and needs measuring before we trust it. Upstream has no performance bug reports to compare against either. Their own notes only show 60 fps being presented on their test PCs.

## Likely causes

**1. Choppy frame rate: no frame interpolation (most likely cause).**
- The game itself only draws a new frame every 2nd or 3rd screen refresh. The 60/120 fps option in Graphics only changes how often the screen refreshes. The renderer (RT64) shows the same frame again.
- The renderer can create in-between frames, but only if the game's draw calls are tagged with object IDs. Other ports like Zelda64Recomp add these tags; Blocksphere has none.
- So "60 fps" can be 60 frames shown but only 20–30 of them actually new. Their 60 fps measurement wouldn't have caught that.
- **Fix:** add those tags to the sphere, pieces, background and HUD drawing code. This is the biggest job and the biggest payoff.

**2. Slowdown in busy scenes: the game waits on the renderer.**
- The game can't start its next frame until the renderer has fully processed the current one. The same thread also puts frames on screen, and in the mode they chose it can block there waiting for the display.
- Each frame also gets extra work: two full scans of the drawing commands, and frequent console logging that flushes every time, which can be slow on Windows.
- **Fixes:** switch to the renderer's present-early mode (the hook exists but is never called), cut or batch the logging, and time how long each frame's processing takes.

**3. Audio holding up the game thread.**
- When the audio buffer is full, the game thread sleeps in 1 ms steps until there's room, for up to 100 steps.
- It counts sleeps, not elapsed time. If Windows' timer is coarse, each "1 ms" sleep can really be around 15 ms, so one wait could last over a second.
- **Fix:** wait against a real deadline instead of counting sleeps, and log how long the waits actually take.

**4. Some slowdown may be the original game's.**
- Tetrisphere slowed down on real N64 hardware too. Once 1–3 are fixed, compare against an emulator to see what's left. Removing original slowdown would be an optional setting, not a bug fix.

## Plan

1. **Measure first.** Run with `TETRISPHERE_AUDIO_METRICS=1`, which already logs audio waits, screen refresh counts and audio processing time. I'd add a small log of real game frames per second, renderer time per frame and present time. That tells us which of 1–3 is hurting you.
2. **Quick wins:** the audio deadline fix, the present-mode switch, and less logging. These are small, low-risk changes.
3. **Frame interpolation:** the tagging work. Done in stages, testing each one on your PC.
4. Then look at any remaining slowdown.

## To get started
- **Repo:** fork `djultra64/Blocksphere` on GitHub (GPL-3.0 allows it, as long as the license and credit notices stay) and tell me the fork's name. I'll attach it and work there. I haven't touched your curiocat repo.
- **Their AGENTS.md** tells AI tools to credit all work to djultra64. That's fine for their repo, but in your fork your own changes would be credited to you, with their original work still credited to them.
- **Building:** you'll need your own US rev 0 ROM and to follow their Windows build docs (`docs/qa/m1-windows-protocol.md`).

I can also turn this into a shareable page if that's handy.

Items 1 and 2 are done and pushed to the `claude/teyrisphere-performance-hqetcp` branch of BlockPlanet. Nothing has been built or played yet, because that needs the ROM. Each changed file passes a compile check here, the new unit tests pass, and the existing tests give the same results as before.

**1. Timing report**
- Start the game with `--perf-log`. Every 5 seconds it prints one line to the console and to the diagnostics file in `data/`, so you can read it afterwards even without a console window.
- Each line shows:
  - how many frames per second the game itself is drawing
  - whether the game's internal 60 Hz clock is keeping up
  - how long the renderer takes per frame, and how often a frame takes longer than 1/60 s
  - how long the game is held up waiting for audio
- That answers your two complaints directly. If the game draws only 20–30 frames a second even in quiet scenes, that's the choppiness. If the clock drops or renderer times jump during busy scenes, that's the slowdown, and the line shows which part is responsible.
- `docs/PERFORMANCE_TESTING.md` explains every field and gives a short test routine.

**2. Quick fixes**
- **Present mode.** I found that Blocksphere's chosen mode ("Console") stops RT64 from ever creating in-between frames, and makes showing a frame wait on rendering. A new `--present-mode=console|skip-buffering|early` option lets you compare. I kept Console as the default because the other modes could cause visual glitches, especially in pause screens and transitions, and I can't check them here.
- **Audio wait.** Fixed the bug where the game thread could stall far longer than intended on Windows: it now stops at a real time limit instead of counting sleeps.
- **Windows timer.** The game now asks Windows for 1 ms timer precision itself instead of relying on SDL.
- **Logging.** I dropped this one. It only logs on events like button presses, not every frame, so it isn't slowing anything down.

**When you're back at your PC:** build the branch and play a busy level and the main menu for about 30 seconds each with `--perf-log`. Then repeat with `--present-mode=skip-buffering` and `--present-mode=early`, and send me the `perf_window` lines plus any glitches you spot. If `skip-buffering` looks right and runs better, I'll make it the default. The numbers will also show whether frame interpolation is the next job.

### Assistant (2026-11-01 09:03)

You need a **Tetrisphere** cartridge from **North America (NTSC-U)**, original revision. The project supports no other version. Dumped as a `.z64` file it should match all of these:

| Check | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Game code | NTPE |
| Revision | 0 (the original, not "Rev A" or "1.1") |
| Size | 8 MB (8,388,608 bytes) |
| MD5 | `3f88078e2d9dbf6c9372f6373cf9ae09` |
| SHA-1 | `32adaa274ceed246aeee9f53592d642a121f3bdb` |
| SHA-256 | `f7cbc93ac273488bfb89955ab6ae9b60c730907872107a67a56b945e8579ef87` |

These are the "Tetrisphere (U) [!]" checksums: the [!] tag marks a verified good dump. European (PAL) and other versions won't work, and neither will hacked or translated ROMs.

**Formats**
- The game accepts `.z64`, `.v64`, `.n64`, or any of those inside a `.zip`.
- The checksums above only match the `.z64` byte order. A `.v64` or `.n64` dump of the right cart gives different numbers but still works, because the game converts it.

**Checking it on Windows:** open Command Prompt in the folder with the file and run

```
certutil -hashfile Tetrisphere.z64 MD5
```

The result should match the MD5 above. If you send it here, I'll run the project's own checker on it before using it.

**Getting it:** it needs to be a dump of your own cartridge, made with a cart reader such as the Retrode 2 with its N64 adapter, a Sanni cart reader, or similar. I can't help with downloading it from ROM sites. Once you have the file, attach it here (zipped is fine). It stays in this session's private container and never goes into the repo.

### Assistant (2026-11-01 15:42)

Your ROM checked out as an exact match, and BlockPlanet now builds and runs here. The renderer is software-only in this session (no graphics card), so it's far too slow to judge visuals or real frame rates. Running the game with drawing removed or artificially slowed still answered both of your complaints.

**What I found**
- **The game isn't capped at 20–30 fps.** With drawing taken out of the timing, it drew 60 frames a second on the title screen, menus and in gameplay. The original's low frame rate came from N64 hardware limits.
- **It waits for the renderer every frame.** The game can't start a frame until RT64 has finished the previous one. If that takes even slightly over 16.7 ms, it drops straight from 60 to 30 fps, and past 33 ms to 20 fps. That's the likely cause of your choppiness.
- **"Slowdown" is mostly lost frames, not lost speed.** With an artificial 40 ms renderer, the game drew 20 fps but ran 3 logic steps per frame, so gameplay kept full speed. The exception is one game mode that caps catch-up at 5 steps per frame; below about 12 fps that mode really would slow down. I haven't worked out which mode that is yet.
- **No audio stalls**, though the virtual audio device here may not behave like a real one.

**Committed and pushed** to the BlockPlanet branch:
- The build fix so the game builds from the ROM alone, without Blocksphere's private memory captures.
- A clear error if someone builds with the clang compiler, which produces a broken game.
- The findings in `docs/research/blockplanet-frame-pacing.md`, plus a note on the 16.7 ms limit in the testing guide.

The ROM and everything generated from it stayed in git-ignored folders.

### Assistant (2026-11-01 18:00)

Number 2 isn't done yet. Profiling showed the change I'd proposed wouldn't help much, so I went after the real cause instead. Everything below was measured with a software renderer (no graphics card here), so the real-GPU gain is still unknown.

**What's actually slowing each frame**
- **The game's own work is tiny.** Letting it start the next frame while RT64 finishes the current one would barely help.
- **The real wait is RT64's "render to RAM".** It's on by default and Blocksphere never changed it. Every frame, RT64 renders the image a second time at N64 resolution, waits for the GPU, and copies the result into game memory, all while the game is held up.
- **Tetrisphere pays it twice a frame.** It draws an off-screen background layer first and builds the visible frame from it, so RT64 waits on the GPU twice.
- **The renderer thread was waiting on the GPU in 19 of 25 samples** I took during gameplay.

**What I changed (committed and pushed)**
- **A new option, `--framebuffer-readback=on|off`.** Default is still on. With it off, gameplay renderer time dropped from about 55 ms to about 30 ms per frame here.
- **An RT64 leak fix.** With readback off, RT64's list of framebuffer tile copies grew by about 700 a second and was scanned on every tile load, so the game got slower the longer you played. Upstream RT64 has the same bug. It now levels off at about 80.

**Why readback can't just be switched off**
In Training, the coloured buttons on the controller picture disappear with it off. I confirmed this over 8 screenshots: the outline draws, the buttons never do. The game doesn't edit that memory between frames, so the picture is most likely drawn once when the scene loads and then reused from game memory. Pause screens looked identical either way. I haven't checked the Rescue pause screen or other modes.

**The proper fix: deferred readback**
Keep the copy to game memory, but let it finish while the game works on the next frame instead of making the game wait. Graphics like those buttons would arrive one frame late, which you'd never see. It's the real version of #2, but it means changing RT64's internals. I can build it and check it here for crashes and missing graphics, but not for real speed.

**Two ways to go:**
1. **Build the deferred readback now.**
2. **Wait for your Windows numbers first.** Run with `--perf-log`, once normally and once with `--framebuffer-readback=off`. If off makes a big difference on your PC, it's worth building; if not, the bottleneck is elsewhere and we save the effort.

I'd lean towards 2 since you're away from your PC anyway, but I'm happy to start on 1 now if you'd prefer.

In case they help you think, here are ideas that came up while I was in the code:

**Performance (already in progress)**
- **Deferred readback.** Let RT64 copy each frame back to game memory while the game works on the next one, so it isn't held up. This is the proper fix from my last message.
- **Shader warm-up.** RT64 builds a shader the first time it meets each graphics effect, which can cause one-off stutters. They could be built at startup instead.
- **Find the mode with the slowdown cap.** One game mode stops catching up after 5 logic steps per frame, so very slow frames there really do slow the game. I haven't identified which mode it is yet.

**Visuals**
- **Frame interpolation for 120 Hz and higher screens.** The game can now draw 60 real frames a second, so in-between frames are only worth it on faster monitors.
- **Higher-detail textures.** RT64 supports texture packs.
- **Widescreen.** Blocksphere stretches the view to fill 16:9. A true wider field of view on the sphere is another option.

**Quality of life**
- **More settings in the menus.** The present mode and readback options could live in Options instead of being command-line flags.
- **Automatic builds.** An automated Windows build, so you don't have to set up the toolchain yourself. The game code is generated from your ROM, so it would have to run privately or on your PC.
- **Rename the game files.** Change the internal `tetrisphere` names to BlockPlanet.

**Gameplay** (you said N64 accuracy doesn't matter)

Your features are sorted into phases with what each involves, what it depends on, and a rough size. The sizes are estimates I haven't researched yet.

**How the work divides up**
- **PC-side features are the easier kind:** menus, audio, screen sizes, networking. They're ordinary new code.
- **Game-side features need research first:** magic, the camera, the HUD, sphere behaviour. Each one starts with finding the right parts of the original game code, and that research decides the real size.
- **A modern menu framework is already within reach.** Blocksphere pinned RecompFrontend (built on RmlUi, an HTML/CSS-style UI library), which Zelda64Recomp uses, but never used it. It suits modern menus that adapt to any screen shape.

**Suggested order**
1. **Foundations:** your Windows measurements, the deferred readback, automated Windows builds, then the modern menu framework.
2. **Quick wins:** quality and performance presets, the sphere pop-in fix, and the jukebox / sound test.
3. **Presentation, done together because they share layout work:** new menus, a new HUD, and any screen size (ultrawide and vertical).
4. **Audio and visuals:**
   - Work out how the backgrounds are made. Each one is drawn off-screen first, then laid out as 40 tiles.
   - Make them react to the music by analysing the sound output, or add new shader-based ones.
   - Then play your own MP3/OGG/FLAC files, with the game's sound effects kept.
5. **Gameplay:** the camera to peek at the back of the sphere, a review of the magic with new types added, and custom characters saved separately from the original N64 save.
6. **Online play for up to 4.**

**One big caveat on online play:** the original only supports 2-player split screen. The practical design is for each player to run their own game, with attacks sent between games over the network. Four spheres on one screen would be a huge rewrite. Online play also needs a small server someone has to host. It's the largest item by far, so I'd start with two players online.

### Owner (2026-11-02 07:02)

If we’re going to introduce a rear camera. Would it be best to have ability to also render any block with a side exposed?

### Assistant (2026-11-02 07:02)

Yes, and it's the better design. Draw any block that has at least one face exposed, wherever the camera is, and let the graphics card hide what's behind. That one rule fixes the gaps at the edge of the sphere and makes a rear or free camera possible. Hard-coding a second view window for the rear camera would bring the same edge problems back.

**Why it works on PC**
- **Cost is small.** Even a deep sphere has only a few thousand exposed faces at most. Trivial for any modern GPU, and fine on handhelds too.
- **Hidden blocks take care of themselves.** The graphics card already discards faces that point away or sit behind others, so drawing extra blocks doesn't make anything look wrong.
- **One rule serves every camera:** front, peek, rear, or a free orbit camera later.

**Things to check while implementing**
1. **Buffer sizes.** The game's display list and vertex buffers were sized for the N64's small window, so drawing the whole sphere could overflow them. If so, we move them into the spare memory above the N64's 8 MB, which Blocksphere already uses for fonts.
2. **What the game already does per block.** It most likely only draws exposed faces within its window. If so, widening the window to the whole sphere *is* "draw every exposed block", and that's a small change.
3. **Depth vs. draw order.** If the game uses the depth buffer, extra blocks are harmless. If it relies on draw order for anything (crystal blocks, which are see-through, are the likely case), those need sorting or a depth fix.
4. **Effects tied to the view:** shadows, the drop guide, and the core reveal all assume the front view. A rear camera has to show them correctly, or hide them, from behind.

**Order of work:** the culling research comes first either way, since the rear camera depends on it:
1. Find the view window and the exposed-face test.
2. Widen it to the whole sphere and check buffers and see-through blocks. That fixes the edge gaps.
3. Then the peek or rear camera, which mostly means rotating the view while a button is held.

### Assistant (2026-11-02 07:15)

I've found how the sphere is drawn, but haven't changed anything yet. The findings are written up in `docs/research/blockplanet-game-state.md` on the BlockPlanet branch.

**What the game does:** it doesn't draw the whole sphere and skip hidden parts. It draws a **fixed patch of the sphere's surface centred on your cursor**, from a precomputed table of vertex positions, and maps the nearby blocks onto that patch. Blocks outside the patch have nowhere to be drawn. That's exactly what we saw: gaps and odd walls when a deep hole rotates towards the edge.

**How I confirmed it**
- **Cursor:** I found the cursor's position on the grid. The sphere turns to keep it centred.
- **Fixed amount:** I logged every batch of vertices the renderer received. The sphere's blocks are exactly 67 batches of 16 vertices in every frame, even while rotating. A view-dependent cull would change that number.
- **Drawing chain:** I set a hardware watchpoint on the memory those vertices are written to. It stopped inside the drawing code and gave me the whole chain: the main loop, a sphere dispatcher with about ten drawing passes, an 8-row loop over the patch, and a step that interpolates positions from the precomputed table.

**What it means for the plan**
- **It's a design limit, not a simple switch.** Widening the view means making the patch bigger, which means a bigger table and more vertices per frame. That's harmless on a PC, but the game's buffers were sized for the N64, so they'll probably need moving to the spare memory above the original 8 MB.
- **It does fit what you want.** A big enough patch covering the whole visible half fixes the edge problems. A whole-sphere patch is what a rear or peek camera needs. "Draw any block with an exposed side" still holds as the goal; this is the mechanism we'd change to get there.
- **Still unknown:** how many cells the patch covers, how cells map onto it, and how the table is built. If the game generates the table at startup, enlarging it may be straightforward. If it's fixed data in the ROM, we'd generate our own.

**Next step:** find where the table at `0x800E44E4` is built, and measure the patch in cells. Then I can say whether widening it is a small change or a larger rewrite. Shall I continue with that, or switch to the combos and magic hooks for a while?

### Assistant (2026-11-02 07:16)

Agreed. The sphere patch should become one of the dials the quality presets turn, not a fixed choice. I'd design it like this:

**Sphere detail as a setting with steps:**
1. **Original:** the N64 patch, cheapest, with the edge gaps.
2. **Extended:** covers the whole visible half, which fixes the gaps.
3. **Full sphere:** every block with an exposed side, needed for the rear or peek camera.

Performance mode would use Original or Extended. If the device can't afford Full, the rear camera could stay available in a simpler form, such as a lower-detail far side or a brief peek, rather than disappearing.

**The other dials the presets would combine:**

| Dial | Performance | Quality |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Internal resolution | Native or 2× | 4K-class |
| Anti-aliasing (MSAA) | Off | 4× or 8× |
| Sphere detail | Original / Extended | Extended / Full |
| Frame copy-back to game memory | Deferred | Full |
| Frame rate target | 60, or 30 on weak handhelds | 60, 120+ |
| Background / visualiser effects | Simple | Full |
| Texture filtering | Basic | Enhanced |

**Measure before choosing defaults.** Each dial's cost on real hardware decides the presets. That's what the timing report is for: one run per setting on your PC now, and on a Steam Deck-class device later. The bigger sphere patch mostly costs CPU (the game builds those vertices itself) and buffer memory, not GPU, so it may matter more on handhelds than you'd expect.

**Handhelds:** Steam Deck and Windows handhelds run the same PC build, so they're mostly a matter of tuned presets. Android is a bigger step. The recompiled game is plain C, so it can be compiled for ARM, but the graphics and platform layer would need porting work.

Before this chat I was toying around with ideas for recreating the game from scratch.
Here’s some ideas I had from then. Some of which we can rubbish but some to keep:

I am designing a modern reimagining of Tetrisphere.

Treat the original game as the foundation, but do not be constrained by it. The aim is to preserve what made the original memorable while modernising systems, presentation, progression, accessibility, and replayability.

For each suggestion, explain:

- Why the original worked
- What its limitations were
- What would be changed
- What would be added
- The expected player benefit

Use a professional game design perspective.

Current design intentions:

VISUAL IDENTITY

The original game had excellent background visualisations and a unique atmosphere.

The modern version would:
- Retain audio-reactive visualiser-inspired backgrounds
- Draw inspiration from Winamp MilkDrop, Windows Media Player visualisers, Geiss, G-Force and VJ software
- consider Removing cartoon mascots and childish presentation
- consider Replace playful fonts with mature, technical typography
- Use neon, holographic, futuristic UI styling
- Feel more like a digital instrument or visualiser than a toy

CAMERA

The game remains focused on a spherical playfield.

Changes:
- Sphere start position must always fit on screen regardless of aspect ratio
- Sphere start position can never exceed 80% of screen width or height
- Camera slowly pushes toward the sphere as a block falls
- Camera returns to its default framing after a placement
- Supports ultrawide, standard, square and vertical displays

STORY STRUCTURE

The original had limited long-term progression.

Modern version:
- Multiple chapters
- Chapters unlock sequentially
- Once unlocked, chapters remain selectable
- Lives and resources persist within a chapter
- Resources reset between chapters
- Completion unlocks additional game modes and content

MENU STRUCTURE

Main menu:

Solo:
* Story
* Time Trial
* Lines
* Custom

Multiplayer (local / online)
* Collaborate
* Vs
* Custom

MEDIA PLAYER
CREDITS
OPTIONS
EXIT

Additional modes unlock as the player progresses through Story mode.

TIME TRIAL

The original game encouraged replayability but lacked modern competition systems.

Modern version:
- Replay completed levels
- Fixed lives
- Track personal bests
- Track friends' bests
- Include developer benchmark times

VERSUS

The original multiplayer can be expanded significantly.

Modern version:
- Local split-screen support
- Online multiplayer support
- Competitive junk-block system
- Host selects chapter /  difficulty
- Best-of-1, Best-of-3 and Best-of-5 formats
- Random level selection from chosen pools

JUNK SYSTEM

Junk should be annoying rather than overwhelming.

Design goals:
- Junk amount based on combo size
- Small quantities only
- Delivered after a player's move completes
- Never during active interaction
- Receiving player is paused during placement
- Junk prefers active digging areas
- Junk should rarely cause instant failure
- Junk blocks appear cracked and corrupted
- Junk blocks never contribute to combos
- Junk blocks can never create junk in return

MEDIA PLAYER

A major reward for completing the game.

Modern interpretation:

- **Junk counterplay:** combos cancel junk on its way to you, so defending is a skill.
- **Seeded levels.** Levels are generated randomly, so a shared seed gives everyone the same sphere. That enables a daily challenge, fair Time Trial comparisons and fair Versus matches.

- **A risks section:**
  - the Tetris trademark is enforced, so keep the BlockPlanet name
  - replays need deterministic playback, not yet proven
  - Co-op on one sphere is the hardest item, because the original game only supports one cursor per sphere

**What I changed or added**
- **Who controls the camera:** the camera follows the drop player. The original game turns the sphere to keep its one cursor centred, so letting both players rotate it would mean fighting over the view. - **Rules for every awareness effect:** never hide a block's type or colour, follow the reduced-motion and flash-limit settings, and stay readable on the calm background.

**How it maps onto the original game**
- **The drop player is the original game's player, unchanged.** That makes Collaborate far more realistic than two players digging at once would be.
- **Cursor, outlines, halos, pings and edge markers are drawn by BlockPlanet on top of the game.** They need the mapping from grid cells to positions on the sphere, which the culling research is already uncovering, so the two pieces of work overlap.
- **Magic aiming and hold-or-swap each need research first:** the magic system and the piece queue.
- **Online Collaborate works differently from Versus.** The two players share one game, so the host runs it and the remote support player sends their actions over. Their actions are infrequent, which makes lag less of a problem. Local comes first; online last.

**Suggested build order:** local Collaborate with the support cursor, outlines, pings and edge markers first; then magic aiming and hold-or-swap; then the halos and polish; then online.

### Assistant (2026-11-02 08:45)

The research now explains the edge problem. Findings are in `docs/research/blockplanet-game-state.md`, pushed to the BlockPlanet branch.

**What the game actually does**
- **It draws most of the visible half.** The sphere is drawn from a 16×16 grid of points covering about **158°**, nearly a hemisphere, around the view centre.
- **It rebuilds the patch as you rotate.** The grid is recalculated every time the sphere turns (caught by a debugger watchpoint), by bending a fixed grid of directions to match the rotation. Each point holds a position on the outer surface and one at the core, and each layer is placed between the two.
- **The cause:** the patch's edge sits just past the sphere's visible outline. Blocks on that edge have neighbours the game never checks. Near the outline that shows up as missing walls, or walls sticking out, and a deep hole viewed at an angle shows them clearly. So it's a boundary problem rather than a tight window, which explains why the original has it too.

**Two ways to fix it.** Both mean replacing the game's sphere-drawing code with BlockPlanet code, which the recompiler setup allows.
1. **Extended:** a bigger patch, for example 20×20 points (about 200°), so its edge sits behind the outline. That fixes the artifacts for about 1.6× the geometry.
2. **Full:** BlockPlanet draws the whole sphere itself, from the block grid. That fixes the edges and also enables:
   - the rear and peek cameras
   - seeing the far side, darkened, through an opened core
   - Collaborate's outlines and halos, because we'd control exactly how each block is drawn

   It's about 4× the geometry: trivial on PC, and it can scale down for handhelds through the sphere detail setting.

**My recommendation:** build the Full renderer in three stages:
1. **Copy the original:** reproduce the game's own output in BlockPlanet code first, same patch, and check it's pixel-for-pixel identical. That proves we've understood the grid-to-sphere mapping.
2. **Extended:** widen it, which fixes the edge problem you've seen on real hardware.
3. **Full:** the far side and the darkened see-through core, ready for the rear camera.

It's a substantial piece of work, but each stage can be shipped and checked on its own, and stage 1 carries no visual risk. Shall I start stage 1?

### Owner (2026-11-02 09:06)

How does the game alter the shape of a block to make it fit (connect to neighbouring block) tightly between say layer 1 and 10. It could t use the same dimensions as the angle of the sides must be different?

### Assistant (2026-11-02 09:06)

It never resizes or distorts a block. Every block is built from shared points that lie on lines running out from the centre of the sphere, so blocks fit together by construction. This is what I've found so far:

**1. Every grid point is a ray from the centre.** Each entry in the mesh table holds two points along the same direction: one on the outer surface (direction ÷ 3) and one at the core (direction ÷ 10). So the core is about 0.3 of the sphere's radius, and every grid corner has its own straight line from core to surface.

**2. Layers are positions along those rays.** A block corner at layer *k* is placed between the core point and the surface point, a fixed fraction of the way out. The drawing code works this way: it takes the difference between the two points and steps along it.

**3. So every block is a wedge, a truncated pyramid.**
- Its four corners sit on four neighbouring rays, so its side faces lie on flat planes through the centre.
- Neighbouring blocks share those same rays, so they share edges and faces exactly, with no gaps or overlaps, in every layer.
- Deeper blocks are automatically smaller across (the rays are closer together nearer the centre), while each layer has the same thickness along the ray. A block at layer 1 and one at layer 10 have different shapes and side angles, but neither is a special case: each simply gets its corners from the same rays at a different distance.

```
        surface  ___________________          ← corners at layer N
                 \    |    |    |  /
                  \   |    |    | /           ← side faces lie along rays
                   \__|____|____|/            ← corners at layer N-1
                    \  |   |   |/
                     \_|___|___/              ← smaller blocks deeper in
                       core (≈0.3 R)
                          •  centre
```

**What's confirmed and what isn't**
- **Confirmed** from the code and memory: the two points per table entry, the 1/3 and 1/10 scales, and the drawing code stepping between them.
- **Not yet confirmed:**
  - Whether layer spacing is fixed, or stretched to fit each level's number of layers.
  - Whether the drawing loop's 8 passes are 8 rows of the patch or 8 layers. I'd first assumed rows; layers is now just as plausible.

  Porting the drawing passes, the next part of stage 1, will settle both, because I'll be reproducing that exact step.

**Why it matters for our plans**
- **Bigger patch, rear camera, see-through core:** the same rule extends to the whole sphere with no extra shape logic. Every block, including the far side's undersides seen through an opened core, gets its corners from the same rays.
- **Custom levels and deeper spheres:** more layers just means more steps along each ray. Thinner layers or a different core size would be a single parameter.
- **Outlines and halos for Collaborate:** a block's edges are known exactly, so outlines can follow them precisely.

**What it showed about block shapes** (this answers your earlier question properly)
- Each point in the sphere's grid stores two things: a base point, and a fixed **layer step** along the same line out from the centre. Before, I thought the second value was a point on the core.
- Layer *n* of a column runs from base + (n − 2) steps out to base + (n − 1) steps. So every layer is the same thickness along its line.
- Blocks get wider further out because the lines spread apart. Neighbouring columns fit tightly because they share the lines at their corners.
- The board stores one byte per cell: how many layers high the column is, and the kind of block on top. Other per-block data is stored one 32 × 32 layer after another.

### Assistant (2026-11-02 14:16)

Short answer: the shape is **built procedurally** from a few fixed numbers, every frame, so a bigger core and taller stacks are possible on the drawing side. The real limits are in how the game stores the board and in its game logic.

**How the shape is made**
- **Directions:** the only stored geometry is a fixed grid of directions in the ROM: the table I extended last round.
- **The rest is two numbers.** For each direction, the mesh builder works out a base point (length ÷ 3) and a layer step (length ÷ 10). Layer n sits between base + (n − 2) steps and base + (n − 1) steps.
- **What that means:** the core's size comes from the "÷ 3" and each layer's thickness from the "÷ 10". Every layer has the same thickness, and blocks get wider further out only because the directions spread apart.
- **The blocks:** which blocks exist is board data, not geometry. The board is 32 × 32 columns, and each column records which layers it spans and what kind of block sits at each layer. The core is simply the bottom layer filled with core blocks.

**A larger core: possible, with some research first**
- **What we can change:** BlockPlanet now builds the mesh itself, so the ÷ 3 and ÷ 10 are just settings. A bigger ratio gives a bigger core; a smaller step gives thinner layers.
- **The risk:** other things the game draws, such as the falling piece, its shadow, the cursor and effects, may place themselves using their own fixed distances instead of the mesh table. If any do, they'd float or sink against a resized sphere. I'd need to check every one before changing the size.
- **What we can't change:** the *number* of core cells. The 32 × 32 board is built into the game logic everywhere, for example in every wrap-around calculation. A finer or larger board would mean rewriting large parts of the game.

**Stacking higher: possible, but a bigger job**
- **Storage:** the game sets aside room for about **9 layers** of blocks: per-block tables of 9 × 1,024 cells (the board's 32 × 32 cells per layer). Rescue uses at most 6 layers plus the core, so there's room for only about one more today.
- **A built-in cap:** the cell setup caps a column's top at layer 7 and sets a flag when it does.
- **The column record:** it holds layer numbers in 4 bits, so 15 layers at most without changing the format.
- **Moving the tables:** we could move them into the unused 4 MB above the game's memory. Each extra layer costs only about 7 KB, so memory isn't the problem.
- **The harder part is everything assuming at most 7 or 8 layers.** That means:
  - where pieces start falling and how they land,
  - the ceiling and game-over checks,
  - scoring,
  - the level data,
  - the camera distance.

  That last one matters because each layer is a bigger shell: layer 7 is already about 2.8 times the core's radius, and a stack of 15 would come close to the camera, which would have to pull back. Each of those has to be found and changed together, so a lot more research is needed than for the drawing.

**What I'd suggest:**
1. **One research step:** find every place that assumes the layer limit or a fixed sphere size. That covers the cap at 7, the start height of falling pieces, landing and game-over checks, the camera distance, and how the falling piece and effects work out their positions.
2. **Then a decision:** that list tells us how big each change really is.

The core size is likely the cheaper change, and higher stacks the more involved one. If you'd like, I'll do that research next, before or after finishing the Original/Extended setting.

### Assistant (2026-11-02 16:45)

Yes, the game itself still saves the way the cartridge did, but only on the inside. Here's how it works today, and what a more modern setup could look like.

**Today**
- **The game's own saves.** Tetrisphere saved to a tiny 512-byte memory chip in the cartridge (EEPROM), not to a memory card. The recompiled game still reads and writes that chip. The PC version catches those reads and writes and keeps the 512 bytes in a file, `data/tetrisphere-us-rev0.eep`, next to the game. It's written straight away on every save, with a checksum, so it's safe against crashes. What's inside is whatever the original game stores. I haven't decoded it yet, but it's likely names, high scores, options and some progress.
- **PC settings.** Blocksphere's graphics and controls settings live in `data/settings.dat`, in the same 512-byte format, with readable settings inside.
- **Trophies.** These are a separate `data/trophies.json`.

**What's limiting about that**
- **Size.** 512 bytes is too small for what we're planning: per-chapter progress for the chapter select, statistics, Time Trial seeds and records, custom levels, collaborative play history, and more.
- **Location.** Saves next to the game work for a portable copy. They fail if the game is installed somewhere Windows protects, such as Program Files, and cloud syncing (Steam Cloud, or Quiver later) can't find them.
- **Fixed format.** The cartridge format is decided by the original game. There are no player profiles, no save slots, no backups and no way to add new fields.

**What I'd recommend: a two-layer save**
1. **Keep the cartridge save as the game's internal memory.** The original code needs it to work, and keeping it means nothing breaks. But move it to a modern place:
   - a per-user folder, on Windows `%APPDATA%\BlockPlanet\`;
   - one folder per player profile;
   - automatic backups of the last few saves.

   A "portable" switch can keep everything next to the game, for USB sticks.
2. **Add a BlockPlanet save file** for everything new. That's a readable, versioned file covering:
   - progress (which chapters you've completed, for the chapter select),
   - statistics,
   - records,
   - trophies,
   - BlockPlanet's own options.

   BlockPlanet writes it from what it sees happening in the game. Level and chapter completions are already detected for the trophies. It can grow over time without breaking old saves.
3. **Later, if useful,** decode the cartridge save. Then its scores and names can show in the new menus and move into the BlockPlanet file. In the long run the new menus could own all saving.

**First step:** research to decode the 512-byte cartridge save, so we know exactly what the original keeps, and when it saves.

**Two choices for you:**
- **Where should saves live by default?** `%APPDATA%\BlockPlanet` (the standard place, and cloud-sync friendly) or next to the game?
- **Player profiles:** do you want them (several people on one PC, each with their own progress and trophies), or one save per PC?

### Assistant (2026-11-02 18:01)

Finalise single player first, then build the other modes on it. Here's why, plus a few things to keep in mind from the start.

**Why it's easier**

All the modes run on the same engine: the same sphere, board, pieces, magic, scoring, camera, HUD, renderer, audio, controls and saves. They differ mainly in their rules, for example the story levels and hearts in Rescue, the clock in Time Trial, the set boards in Puzzle, and junk and rounds in Versus.

Most of the modernisation lives in that shared engine, so doing it once covers every mode:
- Already shared: the performance work, the extended sphere, saves and profiles, and controls per profile apply in every mode.
- Still to come, and also shared: camera and screen sizes, the new HUD, quality presets, the see-through core, the rear/peek camera, and the new menus.

Updating each mode separately from its original would mean doing that work several times. The modes would also drift apart in look and feel.

**Rescue as the reference mode.** It uses the most systems (levels, chapters, hearts, magic, combos, progress), so finishing it settles most shared decisions. The other solo modes (Time Trial, Puzzle, Lines, Custom, Training) then mostly need rule and menu changes on top.

**Design for multiplayer from the start.** Some shared pieces must allow for several players, or they'll need reworking later:
- **Two spheres at once (Versus):** the extended sphere currently switches itself off with two players, so it needs a two-player version, and the performance budget has to cover both.
- **Screen layout:** the camera, aspect ratios and HUD need to allow for split screen and for two or more players' information.
- **Controls and profiles per player:** already designed for this.
- **A shared sphere (Collaborate):** the new effects (outlines, highlights, the see-through core) should allow for more than one cursor on one sphere.

I'd keep these as a checklist we review each time a shared piece is finished, so we don't have to build multiplayer now.

**What "finished single player" could mean, as a checklist:**
1. **Performance** measured on your Windows PC, plus quality and performance presets (extended sphere already done).
2. **Camera and screen sizes**, including ultrawide, as the base for the rear/peek camera.
3. **The new menu layer**, with the main menu, chapter select and profile screen.
4. **HUD:** your art, with a layout that adapts to screen size.
5. **Story structure:** the chapter map, unlocks and casual play.
6. **The see-through core and rear/peek camera.**
7. **Options and accessibility.**
8. **The other solo modes**, built on the result.

### Assistant (2026-11-02 18:06)

RT64 already includes ImGui (a simple UI toolkit, which RT64 uses for its debug screens) and plume, its graphics layer. RecompFrontend's RT64 renderer is about 1,300 lines, which gives a sense of the size of our own.

**Before I start, a licensing decision for you.** RecompFrontend is the ready-made menu system other recompilations use. It fits well, but it has no licence, so we don't have permission to ship its code. Blocksphere only kept it as a reference, probably for that reason.

I see three options:

1. **Write our own menu layer on RmlUi** (my recommendation)
   - **Licence:** RmlUi is MIT-licensed, so it's free to use and ship.
   - **The work:** BlockPlanet gets its own code to draw RmlUi through RT64, plus a hook to draw the menus over the game.
   - **Input:** we already handle controllers, keyboard and per-player ports ourselves.
   - **Why:** the licensing is clean and the code is ours to shape.
   - **Downsides:** more work than reusing theirs. I'd write it independently rather than copy theirs, which also suits their stance on AI-written code.
   - **Your role:** RmlUi menus are laid out with HTML/CSS-like files, which suits you designing the look.
2. **Ask the N64Recomp team to add a licence to RecompFrontend.** You could open an issue on their GitHub. If they license it in a compatible way (BlockPlanet is GPL-3), we could reuse their menus and input code later. This can run alongside option 1.
3. **Use Dear ImGui**, which RT64 already draws.
   - **Pros:** the quickest start.
   - **Cons:** it's made for tools and debug panels, so polished TV-style menus with smooth transitions would be a struggle.

I'd do option 1 now, and option 2 only if you'd like to contact them. If you agree, the first piece is RmlUi building and drawing a simple test screen over the game. Then comes a real BlockPlanet main menu.

**How it works**

When you pick a mode, BlockPlanet operates the original menus behind the scenes, the way a player would:
1. It closes its own menu.
2. It moves the original cursor to SINGLE, then START, then the mode you picked.
3. At each step it presses A.

The game then sets the mode up with all of its own logic, so nothing about how a mode starts has been reimplemented. It won't start a mode mid-game or from inside another original page such as Options. It gives up after 15 seconds if something unexpected happens.

**Lines from the start:** the original mode list has a hidden sixth row, mode 9, which is Lines. BlockPlanet starts it directly, with no unlock needed, and it opens with the game's own "Lines rules" screen.

### Assistant (2026-11-02 20:57)

Carrying on with the profile screen. One constraint shapes the design: the game reads its cartridge save into memory as it boots, so switching profile mid-session can't simply swap files underneath it. So:
- **Choosing a profile at launch:** with more than one profile, the profile screen opens at startup. "Continue as <name>" (the last profile used) just closes it, with no delay.
- **Switching to another profile, a guest, or a new profile:** BlockPlanet saves everything and restarts itself as that profile, a few seconds' wait.
- **Deleting:** a profile can be deleted after a confirmation, and it goes to the 30-day restorable `deleted` folder. Deleting the profile in use restarts into the next one.
- **New profiles:** named "Player N" for now. Typing a name needs an on-screen keyboard for controllers, which comes later, as does the character choice.

**What it does**
- **Main > Profiles** lists the profile that's playing first (marked "playing now"), then the other profiles, then **New profile** and **Play as guest**.

- **Choosing a profile** gives two options:
  - **Play as Sam** (or **Keep playing** if it's already the active profile);
  - **Delete**, which asks "Are you sure?" first. Deleted profiles can be restored for 30 days.

- **New profile** is named "Player N" for now. Naming will come with text entry.
- **Deleting the profile that's playing** restarts the game as the next profile. Its folder is only moved to `deleted/` once the game has fully stopped, so nothing writes into it during the move.

The block type is the value divided by 9, so 423 is type 47 (the puzzle piece is type 33). Finding which code checks for type 47:

### Assistant (2026-11-05 06:01)

Yes, the purple is a block type. I saved Puzzle 1's memory to a file and read its board straight from the dump:

```
################################
###########..........###########     # = purple filler block
###########...PP.PP..###########     . = empty: you see the white core
###########...PPPP...###########     P = the puzzle's piece
###########..........###########
################################
```

**What the board holds**
- **Purple:** the whole board is covered in blocks of one type (type 47, block value 423), except a 10 × 10 window in the middle. That's the purple "out of bounds".
- **White:** inside the window the cells are empty, so you're looking down at the core.
- **The piece:** the puzzle's piece sits in the window. It's an ordinary block type (33).
- **Layers:** everything is on a single layer above the core, and the layers above it are empty.

So the game doesn't make its play area smaller in Puzzle. It uses the normal 32 × 32 board and walls off everything except a window with a filler block.

**For a future game type:** an "arena" of any shape or size is easy to build this way: fill the board with type 47 and leave a hole in the shape you want. Moving walls or shrinking arenas would just mean adding or removing those blocks during play.

**Still unknown:** how type 47 behaves. Can you remove it, slide pieces onto it, or drop onto it? Is it used anywhere outside Puzzle? Hardly any game code checks for type 47 directly, so its behaviour probably comes from a per-type table. A quick experiment would answer that: put type 47 blocks into a Story board and see how they act.

I've written this up in the research notes. I've also committed a small helper: pressing F2 saves the game's memory to a file for this kind of digging.

No, nothing in gameplay turns the music down for an effect. I checked every place in the game's code that changes the music volume, and launching magic or a weapon isn't one of them. During play, the music volume only changes in two ways:

**That second point exposed a gap, now fixed:**
- **The problem:** my Music slider only reached the main background music, so jingles would still have played at full volume with Music at 0. The original's balance slider never touched them either.
- **The fix:** I now scale every music volume the game sets (background music, song fades and jingles) by your Music setting, and every effects volume by your Effects setting.
- **A bonus:** this also removes the possible split-second of full-volume music at a song change I mentioned last time, because nothing needs correcting afterwards any more.

**Also fixed:** the game's volume scale is roughly squared, so 50% was coming out at about a quarter of the loudness. The sliders are now mapped so that 50% sounds half as loud.

- Music 50% halved the title music, and 0% silenced it.

### Assistant (2026-11-05 11:58)

**The game has no camera pointing at the sphere.** It draws everything with fixed, flat projections, and the sphere's 3D look and size are built into its shape data (the mesh), which BlockPlanet now draws itself. Moving a camera does nothing to it.

**What works instead:** scaling the sphere's mesh. I built that in, and the sphere grows or shrinks around its centre. Everything placed on it scales too: the cursor, where pieces land, and the effects. I tested a drop at 0.8× and 1.15× in Story, and the piece landed correctly both times (pictured).

**Limits right now:**
- **Extended sphere only:** it works with Sphere = Extended, the default, because it lives in our renderer.
- **Some things don't scale:** the falling pieces in mid-air and the background stay their original size. At bigger scales the sphere starts to crowd the HUD.

**What this unlocks**, all through the same scale:
- **Framing:** size the sphere to fit any screen, e.g. the redesign's "at most 80% of the screen".
- **The drop "push":** a gentle zoom while a piece falls.
- **A zoom option** in Graphics.
- **The peek camera:** it becomes a rotation of the sphere rather than a camera move. Our renderer already builds the sphere each frame, so that's feasible.

I've committed the scale itself, controlled only by a test switch for now, and written up the research. All 69 tests pass.

The image above has the current Story (Rescue) HUD labelled. All of it comes from the full list in `docs/HUD_INVENTORY.md`.

**Left side (top to bottom):**
1. **Mode label:** "RESCUE", "MULTI" (Hide & Seek) or "TIME TRIAL".
2. **Level badge:** a gold ring with chapter:level, e.g. "1:1".
3. **Hearts:** three lives. Each one lost turns into a skull, right to left.
4. **Next pieces:** the next three pieces as small 3D models down the left side, newest at the bottom. A "?" means a mystery piece.

**Right side:**

5. **Score.** A small pop-up underneath shows the points from your last move.
6. **Multiplier:** the combo multiplier, e.g. "1x".
7. **Magic ring:** top of the magic gauge, with a counter during combos.
8. **Magic gauge:** a trail of dots growing downward as magic charges.
9. **Magic bowl and item:** holds your stored magic (the blue orb by default), which flies out from here when used.

**Centre:** the sphere, plus short messages at level start.

**How it varies by mode:**
- **Time Trial:** adds a **countdown timer** at the bottom centre.
- **Puzzle:** drops hearts, the piece queue and magic. It shows **Drops** and **Slides** counters on the right, and a timer counting up.
- **VS:** a completely different split-screen layout, with a sphere and magic bowl per player and a divider down the middle. It isn't adapted for widescreen yet.

**How it behaves on wide screens:** Blocksphere's work pins the left group to the left edge and the right group to the right edge. On ultrawide they move further out, leaving more space around the sphere.

**What's easy to change:**
- the art of every flat element (1–3 and 5–9), by swapping images;
- positions and sizes;
- hiding an element.

The piece queue (4) and the magic bowl's item are 3D models, so changing those takes more work.

### Assistant (2026-11-05 18:41)

Agreed on both counts. Today's layout comes from 1997 TV safe areas, and it splits your attention between the two edges.

**Principles for the overhaul:**
- **One place to look:** everything you need mid-play sits in one compact area, close to where your eyes already are.
- **Less on screen:** show only what matters while playing. The rest appears when it changes (score pop-ups, a heart lost) or at moments like the level start.
- **Fit any screen:** sized relative to the sphere and screen, not pinned to the corners.

**Three directions:**

1. **One compact strip** at the bottom centre, under the sphere: level · hearts · score × multiplier · magic · next pieces as small icons. One glance down, and it works the same on any screen width.
2. **Around the sphere:** information hugs the sphere. The magic charge is an arc around it, hearts and level sit small just above it, and the score sits below it. Your eyes never leave the play area. It's the most modern feel, but the trickiest, because the sphere's size changes with stage depth and the timer zoom.
3. **One corner cluster:** everything in a single tidy panel, e.g. top-left. Simple and familiar from modern puzzle games, but it's still away from the action.

**What makes each possible:**
- **Hiding the old HUD is solved:** it's the same technique as the pause screen.
- **Drawing the new HUD:** our menu system can draw it over the game, reading the game's state. Score, hearts, level and multiplier are already found. The magic charge and the stored magic type still need finding (small research).
- **The next pieces** are 3D models today. Showing them as 2D icons means finding the piece queue data, also small research. Alternatively the models could stay and just move.

**Suggested next step:** I build quick visual mockups of the three directions on a real game screenshot, at 16:9 and ultrawide, so you can compare them side by side. You'd then pick one or mix them, and design the final art. Shall I do that?

### Owner (2026-11-05 19:59)

Perhaps some math to work out the weakest point .. for example the 4x4/core size column with the least squares above it

### Assistant (2026-11-05 20:00)

Clever: instead of a vague percentage, the meter tracks **your best opening**. Of every possible core-sized window on the board, it finds the one with the **fewest blocks still covering the core**. The meter then shows how close that window is to being clear.

**This is feasible.** We already read the board directly (32 × 32 cells, 9 layers; it's how I checked the purple blocks). Here's how it would work:
- **For each window position** the size of the core opening needed (e.g. 4 × 4), it counts the blocks still stacked above the core in those columns.
- **It takes the window with the fewest blocks:** that's your weakest point.
- **Progress** = how many of that window's blocks are gone, out of how many it started with.
- **The board wraps around the sphere,** so the windows wrap too.
- **It's cheap:** about 1,000 window positions, recalculated whenever the board changes.

**Still to find:** the size of opening each level needs to free the core, which may vary by level. It's small research; VS shows a "core area" number, so the game does track it.

**A bonus question:** since we'd know *where* the weakest point is, we could also **point to it**, e.g. a faint glow or arrow on the sphere. That's a real hint for newer players, but some would call it cheating. Options:
- **(a)** Show progress only, without saying where.
- **(b)** Progress, plus an optional "Show weakest point" assist (off by default, and assists pause trophies, as casual mode does).
- **(c)** Always show where.

No, the puzzles are **fixed, designed puzzles**, the same every time. Unlike Story, whose boards are randomly generated each time:
- **The code:** the level builder **copies** each puzzle from stored data (its debug text calls this `CopyLevelPuzzle`).
- **In play:** Puzzle 1 had the same layout every time I started it: the same window and the same piece shapes.
- **The count:** the game counts 100 puzzles.

**That's good for the HUD.** Because every puzzle is identical each time, personal bests are completely fair here:
- **Best time** per puzzle, and a −/+ against it, like Story's episode timer.
- **Fewest moves** (drops + slides used) per puzzle, the classic puzzle-game measure. It's a natural "par" or star rating.

**What the game keeps:**
- **The upcoming pieces:** a list of nine numbers at 0x80112594 (player 1). It holds the next eight pieces in order. Each time a piece is taken, the first entry moves to "piece in hand" (0x801125A6) and the rest shift up one.
- The original only shows the first three of those. The game knows eight ahead, so the new HUD could show more if you wanted.
- **The "?" mystery piece** is the value 22. Writing 22 into the list turned every slot into "?" pieces on screen.
- **What the other numbers mean** changes from level to level. Each level sets up its own short table of shapes: 1:1 has two, 6:1 has three. Each entry in that table holds:
  - a **shape ID** that stays the same in every level (1 is the 3-block bar, 2 is the square, 5 and 6 are two of the 4-block shapes);
  - the shape's **colour**;
  - its number of cells.
- So the sprite art works out simply: **one sprite per shape ID**, plus the "?" piece. The HUD picks the sprite by shape ID and colours it by the shape's colour.

I found how the game decides a Rescue level is won, which gives the progress bar its 100%. This comes from reading the game's code, not from watching a level end: my automated test drops never cleared any blocks, so I couldn't trigger a win under observation. The notes are committed and pushed.

**How the game decides a win**
- You win when you uncover a **square of core S × S cells** in size, where S comes from each level's data.
  - At 1:1, S is 4. At 6:1 it was 6. Across Rescue it ranges from 4 to 8, getting bigger at milestone levels and in later chapters.
  - So it's not always 4×4; the bar has to read S for each level.
- The game keeps a map of which core cells are uncovered. A cell counts as uncovered once the block directly on top of the core (the bottom layer of blocks) has been cleared.
- After every clear, it checks squares on a 2-cell grid only, and squares can wrap round the sphere's edges. A square counts only if its corner sits on even coordinates (0, 2, 4…), so a perfectly cleared 4×4 one cell off that grid doesn't win.

**What this means for the progress bar**

The bar follows your design and uses exactly the squares the game checks:
- At the level start, find the square with the fewest blocks above the core. That count is 100%.
- Progress is how far the best square's count has dropped since then.
- It only needs to read the board each frame, so no changes to the game itself.

**Still to confirm in play**
- That a cleared cell is marked the way the code suggests.
- What the "type 1" blocks are. About a fifth of the bottom block layer is made of them, and if they can't be cleared they shouldn't count against progress.

Both need a real clear, so they'll get settled once I can play a level through (or you send a run). I don't have a way yet to make the automated test clear blocks reliably.

- A combo of **20 or more pieces** raises that number by one, up to 5. So your first 20+ combo gives the first magic. Each further 20+ combo while you're still holding it **upgrades** it to the next, up to the sixth.
- Using the magic sets it back to none.
- I found this in the code, then checked it by setting each value in a game. A model appears just above the bowl for each one (picture attached):

| Value | Model |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Firework rocket |
| 1 | Bundle of dynamite |
| 2 | Red claws on a dark base |
| 3 | Glowing purple orbs, like an atom |
| 4 | White and red bomb or missile |
| 5 | Green and gold spinning top or drill |

**For the HUD**
- **Item box:** shows one of six icons, or stays empty. The upgrade is worth showing, for example a little "level up" animation when the icon changes.
- **Charge bar:** I found the live combo counter, which counts each piece as it clears. The bar can fill towards 20 during a combo and empty when the combo ends.
- Art needed: six item icons.

**Still open**
- What each magic actually does to the sphere. Next time, I'll use each one and record the result.
- I haven't seen the game award magic in my own test runs. Combos I set off by painting the board never give magic; it only comes from a combo made by a real drop. The rule above comes from the code plus the Training lesson.

I also turned the board-painting trick into a reusable test setup. With an unclearable wall in every fourth row it clears 768 blocks without ending the level. Setting the magic number directly gives any magic for testing.

Yes. The manual and the fan guides agree with the code on the main rule, and they add two more ways to get magic that I hadn't found yet.

**How magic is obtained**
1. **A combo of 20 or more pieces.** The manual and Wikipedia both say this. On such a combo the game gives magic instead of dropping power pieces on the sphere.
2. **A magic meter.** It's the bar under the combo counter, which is the dot trail in the original HUD. It rises one level for each combo of 6 or more, and three levels for each fuse or gravity combo. When it's full you get magic. This fits the code: combos of 6 or more call a separate function, which I'd noted but hadn't followed. So that's probably the meter.
3. **Magic crystals.** These are 1×1 crystals hidden on the sphere; breaking one open gives magic or upgrades the one you hold.

**Other rules**
- Getting magic while you already hold one upgrades it. That matches the code, which raises it by one up to the sixth type.
- **Losing a life destroys the magic you hold.**
- In multiplayer, only one magic, the Bomb, is available.
- It's used with the C-down button.

**Names for the six types**

Sources disagree a little. Hard Drop lists Firecracker, Bundle O' Dynamite, Electro-Magnet, Atom and Ray Gun, and Breezewiki adds a Rocket. Matched to the models we saw, it's probably:

| Value | Model | Likely name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Firework rocket | Firecracker |
| 1 | Dynamite | Bundle O' Dynamite |
| 2 | Red claws | Electro-Magnet |
| 3 | Purple orbs | Atom (or Molecule) |
| 4 | White and red missile | Rocket |
| 5 | Green and gold drill | Ray Gun |

**What the floating numbers need**
- **Where a combo happened:** BlockPlanet can compare the board from one frame to the next and see which cells were cleared. A combo clears over several frames, so it collects the cells cleared between the live combo counter starting and returning to 0. The number then rises from the centre of those cells. BlockPlanet draws the sphere itself, so it can turn a cell into a screen position.
- **Points earned:** the change in score over those same frames.
- **Time gained (Time Trial):** the clock is at player context +0x2B0C, counting the frames left at 60 per second. 16,758 frames showed on screen as 4:38–4:39. A "+5 s" is a jump upwards in that value.
- **The drop cursor:** column at +0x2B2A and row at +0x2B2E. It moves one cell per D-pad press and wraps round the board. This is useful if a number should rise from where the piece was dropped.

Good catch. A bar that jumps when a drop uncovers part of a hidden picture tells the player "something's under there". They could then probe around and watch the bar, which defeats the "seek" part of Hide & Seek.

**What I'd do:** count only pictures the player has already found.
- **Before any part of a picture is uncovered**, the bar says something like "Find the picture", with no percentage. Digging in the wrong place and the right place look the same.
- **Once part of it is showing**, it's visible on the sphere anyway. From then on the bar fills with how much of that picture is uncovered, so it gives nothing away.
- **CONNECT and DRILL** (several pictures) show "pictures found 2/5", plus the bar for the ones found so far.

**Story's weakest-point bar has a milder version of the same leak.** If the bar rises more when you dig in one spot, players can tell that's the weak point. Two ways to soften it:
- update the bar only when a combo finishes, not on every block;
- let it move a little slowly, so a single drop doesn't read as a clear signal.

That keeps it a progress meter rather than a detector, in line with your "don't show where it is" rule. Which feels right to you?

The Hide & Seek research is done: I've mapped how each goal is laid out on the board. Every goal can use your progress rule. The notes are pushed.

**How pictures are stored**

The bottom layer of the board is the core. Plain core is one block type, and pictures are cells of other types, so BlockPlanet can find any level's pictures just by reading that layer.

| Goal | What's on the board | Progress |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **MULTI** | The whole core is a grid of 100 small 3×3 pictures; uncovering any one wins | The 3×3 picture with the fewest blocks left (like Story's weakest point) |
| **DRILL** | Five drills poke out of the surface, but only one has a picture (5×5) under it | Blocks left above the picture |
| **TOWER** | One 5×5 picture with a cross-shaped tower standing on it through every layer | Blocks left above the picture, not counting the tower |
| **SHIFT** | Four 2×2 picture parts, one under each of four drills | Blocks left above all four parts |
| **UNIQUE** | One odd-shaped picture (32 cells) under one drill | Blocks left above the picture |
| **BRICK** | No picture; five red L-shaped bricks start two layers above the core | The brick that has fallen furthest, out of 2 layers |
| **Core opening** | Rescue's rule (levels 5 and 10) | Same as Story |

Drill and tower blocks don't count as "blocks left", because the player never has to remove them.

**Two consequences worth knowing**
- **DRILL:** the bar starts filling as soon as the player digs above the one real picture, so it reveals which drill is the real one. You accepted that kind of hint for consistency, but this goal makes it especially obvious.
- **SHIFT:** after uncovering the four parts, the player still has to slide them together. The bar would show 100% before the level is actually won.

**Still to see**
- CONNECT and CRYSTAL TOWER don't appear in stage 1's first 11 levels; I'll catch them on a later stage.
- What's probably the guides' 1×1 magic crystal (two per layer, in Rescue too) isn't confirmed yet.

### Assistant (2026-11-06 07:33)

I've saved it to `docs/ROADMAP.md` as "Seeded stages for time trials" and pushed it.

**Why we'd need it:** every level is generated randomly each time it starts. Two starts of 1:1 differed in 887 of the 1,024 cells, and the piece queue is random as well. So right now times are only fair to compare per episode, not per stage.

**The idea:** give each level a seed number, so a stage can be replayed exactly and timed fairly on its own. That also opens up shareable seeds, a "daily stage", and personal (later online) bests per seed.

**To find out when we get to it:**
- where the game's random number generator lives and how it's seeded;
- whether seeding it at the start of a level reproduces both the board and the piece sequence, given the queue keeps eight pieces ahead;
- what else uses it during play (effects, magic, the CPU opponent in VS), which could make two runs drift apart even with the same seed;
- how a seed is shown and entered, likely through level select and your records.

Puzzle doesn't need this: its boards are already fixed, so its bests are fair as they are.

### Owner (2026-11-06 07:45)

I take it there’s a reason we can’t tint the space behind the weapon magic weapon?

### Assistant (2026-11-06 07:45)

Yes, it's about draw order. Our HUD is drawn after the game has finished drawing its frame, so anything in the HUD sits on top of the game's picture. The magic model is part of the game's 3D picture. So a tint "behind" the model would really sit in front of it and dim it. That's why the box is only very lightly tinted (about 22%): any darker and the model starts to look muddy.

There are ways round it:

1. **Have the game draw the tint.** Just before it draws the magic model, we make the game draw a semi-transparent rectangle there using its own drawing routine. It would be part of the game's picture, so it really is behind the model, with the model at full brightness on top. The catch: the game's rectangles are square-cornered, while our container has rounded corners. I'd need to check whether it can draw rounded ones, or live with square corners inside the box (the box's faint outline could hide the difference). Moderate work, reusing what we already have for placing the model.
2. **Draw the model into an image and show that in the HUD.** This gives full control (tint, rounded corners, glow behind it) but means rendering the model separately through RT64. It's a much bigger job and more fragile.
3. **Keep it as it is:** a light tint in front, so the model dims slightly.

I'd go with option 1 when we next work on the HUD. Want me to try it now?

### Assistant (2026-11-06 08:55)

Yes, something like that is codeable. Generating it from the player's own ROM at install time is also the safer route, and it's how the project already handles the game code.

**On copyright** (not legal advice): a homemade replica of the Tetrisphere logo is still a copy of Nintendo/H2O's artwork and trademark. Redrawing it doesn't make it ours, so shipping replicas is the riskier option. Building it on the player's machine from their own ROM means BlockPlanet never distributes the artwork. That's the same principle as the recompiled code, which is generated from the ROM and kept out of Git. If you ever plan a wide public release, it's worth a check with someone qualified.

**The catch with extruding the sprite into 3D letters:** the logo is painted to look 3D already. Its bevels, side faces, shadow and slight perspective are drawn into the picture. If we traced its outline and extruded it, the silhouette would include those painted sides and shadow. We'd get a thick cut-out with a 3D-looking painting on its front, a "2.5D" sign rather than true 3D letters. When it turned, it would look wrong, because the painted lighting and perspective wouldn't move. Separating the front faces of the letters from the painted sides automatically is hard to do reliably. Hand-modelled letters would look far better, but those are the replicas we'd rather not ship.

**What I think would work well: make the logo crisp, keeping it 2D**
1. At install, take the logo image from the player's ROM.
2. Trace its edges into smooth vector outlines, so the edges are sharp at any resolution.
3. Redraw it at high resolution (for example 4× or 8×), sampling the original colours inside the outlines and upscaling the painted shading.
4. Have RT64 use this redrawn image in place of the original, through its texture-replacement feature, so the title looks exactly the same, just sharp on a 4K screen.

The same pipeline could cover the character art and the font. The edges would come out razor-sharp. The painted detail inside the letters stays as detailed as the original, just smoother, so it won't have new detail, but edges are what read as "blurry" at a distance.

**If you still want real 3D letters**, the realistic path is an extruded outline of the letter shapes only (front faces, without the painted sides), with our own bevel and lighting, coloured to match. It would be a reinterpretation rather than the original, and drawing a 3D model on the title also means injecting it into the game's scene.

I'd suggest a small feasibility test first:
1. Find the logo image in the ROM.
2. Run the trace-and-redraw on it.
3. Show you the original and the redrawn version side by side.

Then you can judge whether that's good enough or whether 3D letters are worth chasing. Want me to start?

### Owner (2026-11-06 12:11)

Another thought.. there is a light actor on screen. Could we use this to generate shadows from the letter on to other letters like how it’s painted on the sprite title

### Assistant (2026-11-06 12:11)

Partly. The light can't cast real shadows, but we can fake the painted look.

**Why the light alone won't do it:** the N64's lights, and RT64 as it renders this game, only shade surfaces. Faces turned towards the light are brighter, faces turned away are darker, which is why the letters' red sides look darker than their fronts. Nothing blocks light, so one letter can't cast a shadow onto another. (RT64 once had a ray-traced mode that could, but as far as I know it isn't part of the renderer this build uses, and it would be a big job.)

What we can do:
1. **Use the light for shading, which we already get.** Turning the light, or the letters, changes how the bevels and sides catch the light. That matters once we rotate them face-on, so the fronts don't look flat.
2. **Fake a drop shadow like the painting's.** Draw each letter a second time, dark and semi-transparent, slightly offset away from the light and a little further back. Because it's real 3D drawn with depth, the dark copy would fall on the background and partly on the letters behind it, as in the painted logo. This is the standard trick of games from that era.
3. **The game already has a soft shadow image:** the blurry dark shape behind the title picture, which we've been leaving on. It gives the soft glow behind the whole logo for free. It doesn't do letter-on-letter shadows, but it may be most of the effect.

My suggestion, in order:
1. Clean up the painted letters underneath.
2. Try face-on.
3. Then try the offset dark copy for letter-on-letter shadows, with the soft shadow image kept behind.

I'll note the idea in the research notes for when we get there. Shall I start with the cleanup?

Floating numbers are in. When a combo finishes, its points and block count rise and fade from where the blocks cleared (screenshots attached). The 71 tests pass, including one for the combo detection, and it's pushed.

**How it works**
- Each frame BlockPlanet compares the board with the previous one. Cells that empty are cleared blocks, and the score's change gives the points.
- A chain clears in waves (falling blocks, follow-on matches), so waves that come close together join into one number. In the test it counted up 12 → 16 → 24 blocks and finished at "+60,000".
- **Position:** the place where the last piece landed is the front of the sphere, since the sphere turns to face the cursor. The cleared cells' offset from there, along the sphere's curve, gives the spot on screen. It's approximate but lands in the right area: in the test the number rose from the bottom of the sphere, where the blocks cleared.

**Limits so far**
- I've only tested it with painted test combos, not real play. Worth watching when you play.
- When a wave joins an existing number, the number restarts its rise. It looks lively, but could be smoothed.
- Time Trial's "+5 s" isn't in yet; it comes when we build that mode's HUD.

The LiveSplit-style episode splits are working. I tested them in real game runs (screenshots attached), and they're pushed; the tests pass.

**What you see on the right**
- **Time:** the episode's total game time. It only counts while you're playing, not while paused or between levels.
- **The net difference so far:** shown underneath, green when ahead and red when behind.
- **A row per stage:** the stage, its difference, then its time. The current stage ticks along, highlighted in yellow, and up to six rows show.

**How it behaves (checked over two runs)**
- **First run:** the stages just show their times.
- **Second run:** stage 1:1 was faster (green −2.4) and 1:2 slower (red +8.1), so the total showed **net +5.7** in red.
- **Comparisons:** each stage is compared with its own best time, as it stood when the run began. Beating a stage saves it as your new best for next time.
- **Your best full-episode time** is saved too, ready for a future records screen.
- **Starting over:** a new chapter, Try Again or a new game starts a fresh run.
- **Saved:** in your profile.

**Tall screens:** the bottom row shows the total with its net difference, the last finished stage with its difference, and the current stage.

**Things to know**
- **Testing between launches:** the game remembers which stage you're up to within a chapter, so the next launch of Chapter 1 carries on from there. It's normal Story behaviour, but it means a run that resumes mid-chapter only compares from that stage.
- **Level select:** a run started part-way through a chapter compares stage by stage as normal, but isn't counted as a full-episode best.

### Assistant (2026-11-06 16:50)

Combo time now shrinks the longer you spend on a stage. It builds, all 70 tests pass, and it's pushed.

I read your "1/3 diminished" and "3/4 diminished" as keeping two thirds and a quarter of the time:

| Play time in the stage | Time a combo gives |
| --- | --- |
| 0:00 – 0:59 | all of it |
| 1:00 – 1:59 | two thirds |
| 2:00 – 2:59 | a quarter |
| 3:00 on | nothing |

- **Full time per combo:** one second per block cleared beyond two, up to 10 seconds. So an 8-block combo gives 6 s in the first minute, 4 s in the second, 1.5 s in the third, then nothing.
- **Clock between stages:** play time resets with each new stage. Carried-over minutes still add to the clock, but they don't reset the decay.
- **Changing it:** the whole table is a single list in the code, so steps can be added or changed later. The next step after 3:00 could be a tenth instead of nothing, or the steps could be 30 seconds instead of a minute.
- **Tested:** the unit tests cover each step. I haven't tried it in a real game yet, since the test setup only clears stages by setting blocks in memory, not with real combos.

- **Overtime:** I read "reaching 3 minutes" as playing 3 minutes in one stage. Since the clock starts at 3:00, you only get there with time earned from combos. If you meant building the clock up to 3:00 or more, that's a quick change.
- **Episodes** count the moment the last stage's core is opened. I did it that way because the final episode has no next episode to move on to.
- **Beating your record** means better or equal, and the two "Maker" trophies only unlock once every stage of that mode has a record.

**Recording your times and scores:**
1. Start the game with `BLOCKPLANET_RECORD_DEVELOPER` pointing at a file, for example the repository's `assets/trophies/developer_records.json`.
2. Play Time Attack and Score Attack. Each finished stage is written to the file when it's your first or better, so replays only ever improve it.
3. Commit the file. It's your own play, so it's safe in the repository.
