### Assistant (2026-11-06 17:45)

Score Attack's stage time now depends on the sphere's thickness, and Overtime needs 2 minutes beyond it. All 71 tests pass and it's pushed.

**Stage time:** 2:00 for a one-layer sphere, plus 10 seconds for each extra layer. Story's spheres have 1 to 6 layers, so stages get between 2:00 and 2:50. The game sets the layer count when a stage starts, and the clock picks it up from there.

| Layers | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Start time | 2:00 | 2:10 | 2:20 | 2:30 | 2:40 | 2:50 |

Carried-over whole minutes are added on top, and leftover seconds still become bonus points.

**Overtime:** play 2 minutes beyond the stage's own time in one stage. That's 4:00 of play on a one-layer stage and 4:50 on a six-layer one, so it can only be done with time earned from combos.

**In-game check:** stage 1:1 has 1 layer and started at 2:00; after about 21 seconds it showed 1:39. Stage 1:2 has 2 layers and started at 2:10 plus a carried minute, and read 2:58 about 12 seconds later.

**Worth tuning together:** combo time still diminishes by the minute (all, then two thirds, then a quarter, then nothing after 3:00). With shorter stages, that cut-off now falls soon after most stages' time would have run out. If Overtime turns out too hard, those steps or the 2-minute target are the numbers to change.

### Assistant (2026-11-06 22:50)

Yes, it's doable, and I agree it's the better structure: one set of episodes and stages everywhere, with VS as another way to play them. The challenges are research-heavy rather than hard to build.

**What needs solving**
1. **Load Story's spheres in VS.** We don't yet know which level records VS reads. If it picks its record from a table by mode, a small hook can make VS use Story's numbering (episode × 10 + stage), as we already do with other game routines.
2. **10 stages per episode, not 7.** The game ends a VS episode after 7 rounds and a Story episode after 10, by asking a routine for "levels per chapter" by mode. An earlier test of overriding that routine had no effect, so the real count may live somewhere else. This is the main unknown.
3. **Starting at a chosen episode and stage** (for quick play). Story uses a next-stage counter that we now set. VS may use the same counter or its own; we just need to check.
4. **The core size.** VS adds an episode-based amount to the core each player must open. We'd choose between Story's sizes (so a stage is the same everywhere) and VS's (harder duels). I'd use Story's, for consistency.
5. **The computer's skill.** The opponent probably gets stronger with VS's episode number. We'd map Story's episodes onto that, so episode 1 is gentle and episode 10 is the toughest.
6. **Rounds and hearts.** Each stage becomes one round, and losing a round costs a heart, as in VS now. A game over gives Try Again on that episode, as in Story.
7. **Endings and messages.** VS's own scenes after episodes 3 and 5 would be skipped or replaced, since the episode numbers no longer match.

**What you'd get:** Local > Story > Versus > Computer > Episode > **Whole episode** or **one stage**, the same screens as Campaign. It could also have its own records (rounds won, time per stage) and trophies. The same structure would carry over to two human players once that's available.

**How I'd go about it:**
1. Research first: which records VS loads, where it counts rounds per episode, and where the computer's skill comes from. That's memory comparisons and code reading, like the Puzzle and next-stage work earlier.
2. If those all turn out to be simple values or routines we can hook, building it is moderate work: hooks, the menu and HUD wiring, and records.

The risk is item 2: if the round count is tied deeply into VS's own episode flow, it may take longer. I'd find out early in the research.

Shall I start with that research and note the decision in the design docs?

**How it works**
- **The problem:** while we hold the 3D letters, the game never reaches the point where it loads its painted title picture, so the copyright lines had nothing to come from.
- **The fix:** BlockPlanet now loads that picture from your ROM itself. It runs the game's own ROM-reading and decompression code once, from the title hook, into memory the game doesn't use.

H2O Entertainment no longer exists: sources agree it closed in 2001. I'd still leave the notice exactly as it is.

**What the lines are:**
- The first line is a **copyright notice**: "© 1997 Nintendo". The game's copyright belongs to Nintendo, and Nintendo still exists.
- "Game design by H2O Entertainment Corp." is a **credit**, not a copyright claim. A company closing doesn't cancel credits; it's historical fact.
- The second line is a **licence notice** for the Tetris name. The Tetris Company still exists and actively protects that trademark.

**Why I'd keep it unchanged:**
- **It's their notice.** It belongs to the original game, and BlockPlanet shows it from your own ROM. Editing or removing copyright and licence notices is something rights holders tend to take seriously, and in some countries removing that kind of information is itself restricted.
- **A closed company's rights don't disappear.** They pass to someone (an owner, a buyer or a liquidator), so dropping H2O's name wouldn't be safe either.

**What I'd add instead:** a separate BlockPlanet line on the title screen, below or apart from the original notice. For example:
> BlockPlanet is an unofficial fan project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Nintendo or The Tetris Company. Requires your own copy of the game.

That makes clear who made what, without touching the original notice. I'm not a lawyer; if you plan to distribute BlockPlanet widely, it's worth getting proper advice on the wording.

### Owner (2026-11-07 06:24)

The 4mb errors I take it this is a hard coded restriction somewhere.. probs my based on n64 limitations.

### Assistant (2026-11-07 06:24)

Short answer: it isn't a hardware limit and it isn't the port's. It's a sanity check written into the game's 3D scene code, and it's cheap to fix: a few hours, mostly testing.

**What the check is:** the game was written for a 4 MB N64. Its scene code (the LightWave player) tests every pointer it is given against 4 MB, and stops with "detected by LWAllocateMemory" if one points above that. I counted **15 such comparisons**, almost all inside the scene code (`0x8002D108` to `0x8002DD14`, plus one at `0x80026E08`). It's a guard against corrupted pointers, not something the hardware needs.

**BlockPlanet already has 8 MB:** the port runs with 8 MB (the Expansion Pak size), and we already use the upper 4 MB for the sphere's vertex buffers. Only these checks stop the scene code from using that memory too.

**The fix:**
1. Raise the 15 limits from 4 MB to 8 MB. Each is a single constant in one instruction, so it can be changed in the regenerated code from the recompiler config (one setting per spot, no game logic altered).
2. Optionally, give the game's memory pool its own space in the upper 4 MB, so the title (and anything else we add) never competes with the game for its roughly 475 KB.
3. Test: the title, the intro, the credits robots, and a few stages in each mode, to confirm nothing else assumed 4 MB.

**Effort:** a few hours. The risk is low, because the checks only reject pointers; they don't change what the game does with valid ones.

**Other N64 limits worth knowing about:**
- **Already handled by the renderer:** screen resolution, aspect ratio and frame rate.
- **Still present but rarely matter:** the 16-vertex batches and the 4 KB texture memory per draw. Sharper art would run into the texture one; that's mainly for redesigned art, not this.
- **The 8 MB memory itself** could be raised later if we ever need it. The runtime's memory addressing allows up to 16 MB.

Shall I do the 4 MB fix now? It would also simplify the title robots, since their scenes could then live in our own memory instead of the game's pool.

### Owner (2026-11-07 06:33)

I take it the light actor just adds a fake glow. Do you think in time we could have an actual light which brightens up sides of shapes and casts shadows?
This would be good for title letters and possibly even that escape mode I dreamed up earlier  to see inside the sphere

### Assistant (2026-11-07 06:33)

Probably not just a glow, but not real lighting with shadows either.

**What the game has:** the original's lights work the way all N64 lights do. Each scene can have a few directional lights plus an ambient level, and the brightness is worked out once per corner (vertex) of each shape, then blended across the face. So sides facing the light do get brighter, but:
- there are **no shadows**: one object can't darken another;
- lighting is coarse on big flat faces (brightness only changes between corners);
- the "light actor" you spotted is probably a LightWave light turned into one of those directional lights. The glow around it is likely a separate flare effect. I haven't confirmed either; it's a guess from how the format works.

**What's possible, in rough order of effort:**
1. **Better use of N64-style lights (small):** for things we draw ourselves (the ring, rebuilt title parts), we can light every face properly instead of my painted shading, and use the game's own lights on its models. This brightens and darkens sides; no shadows.
2. **Smooth, per-pixel lighting (medium):** done by the renderer rather than per corner, for crisp highlights on the letters and ring. That needs work in RT64, the renderer BlockPlanet uses, or a separate modern pass for our own objects.
3. **Real shadows (large):** objects casting shadows on each other, like the letters onto the ring or blocks onto the inside of the sphere. That needs a proper modern lighting pass. RT64 started life as a ray-tracing renderer, but the version we use is built around faithful N64 rendering, so I'd expect this to mean extending it ourselves. It's feasible, since we control the code, but a project in its own right. I'd want to look at RT64's current code before promising anything.

**For Escape mode:** a light inside the sphere with real shadows is exactly where step 3 pays off. Blocks casting shadows across the inner surface would make depth and holes readable from inside, which is the hard part of that view. Even step 1 (a point of light at the core, faces shaded by angle) would help. BlockPlanet already builds the sphere's geometry itself, which makes the sphere the easiest place to try lighting experiments.

**Suggested path:** do step 1 when we finish the title, and keep shadows on the roadmap, tied to Escape mode, as a renderer research project. Shall I add that to the roadmap?

The robots still draw black, but I now know why, and it's a bigger question than a missing setting. The findings are committed and pushed, the default title is unchanged, and I've stopped here rather than keep going in circles.

**Why they're black:**
- **No colour in the files:** the robot model files carry no usable colour. Every part's colour is black, every vertex colour is plain white, and the parts have no texture. The game draws each part as "part colour × lighting", so black in gives black out.
- **Most parts skipped:** only 26 of Turbine's 123 parts are drawn at all; the rest are skipped by the drawer.

So the game must supply the robots' colours and visibility from somewhere else when it shows them. It might set them in memory, swap in another object, or use a different drawing path. I haven't found which.

**Ways forward:**
1. **Keep hunting (open-ended):** catch the game showing a robot in colour and compare memory. The candidate is the robot sequence I found (`0x8005DA44`), which I haven't seen play yet. It may be the ending, where the rescued robots appear. Getting there in the test setup means playing through to an ending or forcing it, then working out what changes the colours. That could take one session or several.
2. **Draw the robots ourselves (more predictable):** we already decode the meshes. BlockPlanet would draw Turbine, Wheels and the Bombs with its own renderer, like the ring, posed and coloured to match the original picture. The catches: we'd choose the colours by eye from the portraits (your call as art owner), and we'd need to pose the unfolded robots ourselves rather than reuse the game's animation.
3. **Hybrid:** use the game's renderer for the shapes and animation, and set the part colours ourselves, from the portraits or your choice. This depends on fixing the skipped parts, which is less work than route 1 but still some.

I'd go with route 3. It keeps the game's own models and animation, and the colours become a design decision rather than a research hunt. Which would you like?

That reading of the scene makes sense: a core tile blown open, light pouring out, and the robots escaping through it. All of it is possible with what we have, to different degrees.

1. **Bigger, overlapping the ring (easy).** It's a size and position change, plus loosening the clipping so they can sit over the rim.

2. **Turbine looks flat (moderate).** The game's own lights are drawing it, and the scene's lighting seems to be mostly ambient, which flattens it. **Bubble changes**

**Redesign proposal**
1. **HUD at the bottom, in Story's style.** Each element appears only when Wheels introduces it, with a short glow:
   - next pieces, at the shadow page;
   - hearts and the drop timer, at Lives;
   - the progress bar, at the game objective;
   - the combo counter, at Combos;
   - the magic box, at Magic;
   - the X count, in Advanced;
   - drops and slides, in Puzzle.

   The original HUD is hidden in Training, as it is in Story.
2. **Pages combined and scrollable.** Pages that only add more text become one bubble, and A skips past them all. Pages with a demonstration ("Watch") or an animation stay separate, because the game drives those itself. The first page ("Press down or A to page through…") can go, since the "A More" hint says the same.
3. **New steps written by BlockPlanet** for things the lessons never explain: the drop timer, the next pieces, the progress bar, and the Attack clocks. These can pause and explain, but can't demonstrate moves, since the game's demonstrations are its own code.
4. **Wide-screen layout:** a larger, round sphere (needs research into the Training camera), with Wheels and the bubble beside it.
5. **Shorter steps in the Training list:** each lesson's levels as their own entries, such as Moving and Sliding, Lives, Combos and Magic. This needs research into starting Training partway through.

### Assistant (2026-11-08 04:31)

Good questions. Taking them in turn:

**Sharper textures on 3D models.** Your "no HD texture packs" rule rules out shipping replacement artwork. There are still options that work from the player's own ROM at run time:
1. **Better filtering** (Graphics > Texture filter) smooths textures but doesn't add detail. It's already available.
2. **Upscaling by algorithm as textures load:** a pixel-art upscaler such as xBRZ or ScaleFX enlarges each texture 2–4× and keeps edges crisp. Nothing is shipped; it's computed on the player's machine from their ROM, so it fits your rule. This is my recommendation. The work would be a hook in RT64's texture loading.
3. **Replacing textured surfaces with BlockPlanet's own shading,** where a texture is really just a material such as bricks or metal. That's the same idea as replacing sprites with models: more work per item, but sharp at any resolution.

I'll add these to the roadmap.

**The pink.** It isn't a separate pink layer. Training's sphere is a single layer of bricks, one per cell, all of the same kind (they all hold the same value in the game's brick grid). They're identical and sit at the same height, so they merge into one smooth pink surface. Under them, layer 0 is the core, which is the white you see in the pit. In Story there are several layers of mixed brick types, so individual bricks and their edges show.

**The pit's bottom-right corner.** I'll look closely once the current runs finish. I'll compare the brick grid around that corner with what's drawn, to see whether a wall face is missing or one cell sits at a different height.

### Assistant (2026-11-08 10:37)

I ran the Training check with the brick-layer trap, but the stripes didn't appear, so I still haven't found what starts them. The normal game code is back and the findings are committed.

**The trap run**
- Nothing wrote zeros into the band of bricks around the pit. The only removals were inside the pit, which is the game digging it on purpose.
- Including this one, 11 runs of the same Training start have come out clean. The stripes have only shown up in one trapped run so far.

**What removes the bricks when it does happen**
- It's the game's own board checker. Every frame it checks 5 cells, so it covers the whole sphere about every 7 seconds.
- For each brick it works out which piece the brick belongs to and checks that the piece's other cells are still there. If they aren't, it removes the piece.
- In the bad run it failed a filler brick on its very first pass. From then on it removed one more band brick per row on each pass, in a diagonal pattern. That build-up is the stripes.
- In every clean run, all the filler bricks pass the check.
- Ruled out:
  - **The board loading differently:** the board loads identically in good and bad runs.
  - **Leftover memory:** the piece lookup always finds a real answer, so the checker isn't reading leftover memory.

**Still open:** why a filler brick fails that check in some runs. If you see stripes on your PC build, a note of what you were doing just before would help. Until then, the gap filler keeps hiding them.

- The generated code is restored from `functions.orig`, and every file matches the normal manifest again.
- The build points back at that manifest, it's rebuilt, and all 73 tests pass.

### Assistant (2026-11-08 10:52)

That's quite common when building something like this. Antivirus programs often flag new programs that have just been compiled on your own machine, because nothing else in the world has that exact file yet. Here's how to check what it flagged and whether it blocked anything:

1. Open Norton and go to **Security → History** (it may be labelled **Security History**).
2. Find the latest entry and open it. It shows the file's full path and what Norton did (blocked, quarantined, or allowed).

What the path tells you:
- **Inside `C:\Users\<you>\BlockPlanet\`**, for example `.local\m1\toolchain\...\N64Recomp.exe` or `RSPRecomp.exe`: those are the recompiler tools the setup just built from the pinned source. They're expected and safe. If Norton quarantined one, **Restore** it. Then add an exclusion for the `C:\Users\<you>\BlockPlanet` folder only, under **Settings → Antivirus → Scans and Risks → Items to Exclude**. Exclude just that folder, not anything wider.
- **Inside `AppData\Roaming\Python\...\Scripts`** (`cmake.exe` or `ninja.exe`): those are the official CMake and Ninja that pip just installed. Restoring them is fine too.
- **Anywhere else**: tell me the path before restoring anything, so we can check it.

Then look at the PowerShell window:
- If the script is still running, or finished with "Done:", nothing it needed was blocked.
- If it stopped with an error around the time of the alert, Norton probably removed a file it needed. Restore the file, add the exclusion, then run the setup again. Add `-SkipDependencies` if it got past the "Fetching" step.

Paste me the history entry, or the last lines in PowerShell, and I'll tell you which case it is.

### Assistant (2026-11-08 11:00)

That fits. The file is almost certainly `cmake.exe` in `C:\Users\<you>\AppData\Roaming\Python\Python315\Scripts\`.

**Why Norton is wary of it:** when pip installs a tool, it writes a small launcher `.exe` into that `Scripts` folder. The launcher is created on your machine at install time, is unsigned, and has never been seen anywhere else. CyberCapture is built to catch exactly that kind of file, so it flags it.

**Why it's safe:** it's the official CMake package (version 4.4.4) from the Python Package Index. The setup installed it because your Visual Studio didn't include its own CMake.

**What to do:**
- In the CyberCapture window, allow it (**Run anyway** or **Allow**). If Norton had already quarantined it, restore it from **Security → History**.
- Add `C:\Users\<you>\AppData\Roaming\Python\Python315\Scripts` to Norton's exclusions, alongside the BlockPlanet folder. The `ninja.exe` launcher in the same folder will otherwise get the same treatment.

**If you'd rather not exclude that folder:**
1. Open the Visual Studio Installer and choose **Modify**.
2. On **Desktop development with C++**, tick **C++ CMake tools for Windows** and install.
3. Run the setup again. It uses Visual Studio's own signed CMake and Ninja first, and no longer touches the pip copies.

### Owner (2026-11-08 11:06)

will this part take as long for gamers to install?

### Assistant (2026-11-08 11:06)

No. Players never see this step: they download a ready-built package.

**What players do (from the README):**
1. Unzip the release package.
2. Run `tetrisphere.exe`.
3. Choose their own ROM the first time.

That takes seconds. The only other requirement is the Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable, which most gaming PCs already have.

**Why it's slow for you:** you're setting up a developer machine. This runs once and then stays set up. It does the following:
- builds the recompiler tools from source;
- recompiles the whole game from your ROM into C code, which is tens of thousands of functions;
- compiles that code, plus the RT64 renderer and everything else.

**Later builds are much quicker.** After `git pull`, only what changed gets rebuilt, usually a minute or two. If the dependency list hasn't changed, add `-SkipDependencies`, and the game code is only regenerated when the recompiler settings change.

The Norton prompts are also mostly a developer-machine thing, since they were about the tools built or installed here. A released `tetrisphere.exe` is one file that thousands of people run, so Norton learns it quickly.

### Assistant (2026-11-08 11:31)

I think so. You want a highlighted word to mean "this is a game term worth learning". If highlights land on random words, or every mention of everything gets one, players stop noticing them.

**How it works now**
- BlockPlanet has a glossary of game terms (shadow, core, sliding, combo, magic, bricks and so on). The first mention of each term on a page is highlighted.
- The game's own highlights are kept on top of that. Those are uneven: some terms highlighted, some not, sometimes an ordinary word.

**What I'd suggest: one glossary with clear rules, used everywhere** (Training, the cards, How to Play)
1. **Highlight the term where it's introduced or explained.** For example, "This is called **sliding**". It's the strongest cue, and it matches the original's intent.
2. **After that, highlight only its first mention on each page, as a reminder.** Never every mention, so one page doesn't light up with five highlights.
3. **Replace the game's own highlights with the glossary's**, so what's highlighted is consistent, not whatever the 1997 text happened to mark.
4. **Keep the list to real game terms**: shadow, core, sliding, combo, power brick, magic, crystal brick, X count, fuse combo, wildcard, lives, drops and slides. Not ordinary words like "match" or "line up".
5. **Optional later:** show a term slightly differently the first time it's defined, for example with a small glow. Then "new word" and "reminder" look different. The Training HUD reveal could use the same glow.

To set this up I'd need the following from you. It's a short, cheap job.
- A yes or no on the rules above.
- A quick check of the term list. Anything to add or drop?

when i updateblockplanet it seems to be downloading all of the components again, even if they haven't been updated. Is there a better way? assuming i'm correct.

### Assistant (2026-11-08 16:55)

I've pushed a fix. Updates should now be much quicker.

**What was slow:** it wasn't re-downloading. Update skips downloads already. But every run regenerated the whole game from your ROM, and because those files were then brand new, Visual Studio recompiled every one of them. That's tens of thousands of game functions, every time.

**Now:** the update checks whether anything the game code is made from has changed: my recompiler settings, or the recompiler itself. Usually nothing has, so it prints **"Skipped: nothing it is made from has changed."** and only compiles the BlockPlanet files I actually changed. That should take minutes, not most of the run. I can't run the Windows script here, so I haven't timed it on a PC.

**What to expect:** your next **Update BlockPlanet** should already show the "Skipped" line. If I ever change the recompiler settings, it regenerates by itself; you don't need to do anything.

### Assistant (2026-11-08 17:21)

Thanks, that's a useful catch. It's almost certainly BlockPlanet's **Extended sphere**, not the game itself.
- **How it works:** the original game only draws the patch of the sphere near the camera. Extended works out which extra rows and columns to draw around that patch, based on where the camera is looking.
- **What's going wrong:** at the top of the view, the range it picks is a row or two short. So moving up and down slides that edge back and forth, and the bricks at the top pop in and out.

**A quick check that would help:** in **Options → Graphics**, set **Sphere** to **Original** and do the same up and down movement.
- If the top bricks are missing in both positions, or simply cut off at a fixed edge, the popping comes from Extended. I'd then widen its range, or make it always draw the full ring of rows near the visible rim.
- If they still pop in and out, it's the game's own drawing, which is a different fix.

Either way, I've added it to the list. Shall I look into it next, or after the character screen?

see where my shadow is.. what's your understanding of these textured single squares and what i can do with them at this point

### Assistant (2026-11-08 17:36)

Here's what I understand, from the research and Training's text. I haven't played this exact spot, so check it against what you see.

**What they are:** they aren't special blocks. They're ordinary **purple bricks**. Each colour of brick has its own texture, and purple's is a dark tile with a glowing orb in every cell. That's why a purple brick looks like a row of separate squares, while yellow and green look like long smooth bars. So:
- the two side by side on the left are one purple brick, two cells long;
- the 2 × 2 under them is one square purple brick;
- the lone one near the bottom is a one-cell purple brick, or part of one that's partly buried.

**Your shadow:** it's sitting exactly over a purple brick three cells long. That's why those three cells are highlighted. The game marks a brick under your shadow that's the same shape as the brick you're about to drop.

**What you can do there, going by Training's rules:**

### Assistant (2026-11-08 19:06)

**1. No sound effects in the intro.** You're very likely right that they're part of the music. N64 games often build an intro's whooshes and impacts into the music track itself, so it all stays in time with the animation, rather than playing them as separate sound effects. With Music at zero, all of it goes quiet.

To confirm: set **Music to 0** and **Effects to 100**. If the intro is completely silent, everything is in the music. I haven't checked this in the game's sound data, but it matches what you saw.

If it bothers you, a possible later option: play the intro at the music volume even when the music is turned down. That would be just for the intro, so it keeps its sound. Only worth doing if you think people will often play with the music off.

**2. Two players, one with music on and one off.** The audio levels (music, effects, music order) are saved **in each profile**. Only one profile drives the game: **Player 1's**, the one chosen at "Who is playing?". So in local multiplayer, P1's music settings apply. Player 2 has no profile yet; that comes with the multiplayer work.

When we add P2 profiles, I'd keep it this way: whoever is P1 sets the sound, since there's only one set of speakers. Then P2's preference is saved but only used when they play as P1. Does that sound right?

### Owner (2026-11-08 19:11)

Ito confirm.. yes bgm 0 and effects 100.

i don't suppose we could seperate the effects from the music?

### Assistant (2026-11-08 19:11)

Probably yes, with some research. Here's how it would work:
- **How the music is built:** N64 music isn't one recording. It's played live from notes, like a MIDI file, across up to 16 separate **channels**, each playing its own instrument or sound sample.
- **Where the intro's effects are:** the whooshes and impacts are most likely on **their own channels** within the intro's music, using sound-effect samples instead of instruments.
- **The fix:** find which channels those are, then set the volume per channel during the intro. The music channels follow your **Music** level and the effect channels follow your **Effects** level. With Music at 0 you'd still hear the effects, and the reverse.

**What it needs:**
1. **Research:** list the intro track's channels and which sample each plays, to tell the effects from the music. Some channels might mix both, which would limit how cleanly they separate.
2. **A hook** on the game's music player, to set each channel's volume while that track plays. The N64 sound library has a per-channel volume setting, so the game should already support it.

The same trick could work for any other track that has effects built in, such as the endings or cutscenes.

It's a medium job. I'll add it to the list, unless you'd like it sooner.

- Core Gameplay Loop: Phear lacks the N64's combo-building phase. Players cannot "drag" pieces across the sphere to form huge chains. Gameplay is purely high-speed reaction: you rotate the sphere to drop and instantly match current pieces to break down layers to the core.
- Pace: Extremely fast and immediate compared to Tetrisphere.

B. Shape Matrix & Tile Geometry:
Phear did not use standard Tetris tetrominos (I, J, L, O, S, T, Z). It used generic, abstract geometric tiles to slice holes through the layers. Detail the exact geometry profiles of these tiles (e.g., individual blocks, cross-sections, wedges, solid primitive plates) and map out how a block-matching array should behave when a drop event occurs.

C. Color Palette & Layer Separation Shaders:
The original specs list a flat-shaded 16-bit color profile. **BlockPlanet draws the grid itself,** rather than relying on the game's backgrounds:
- **The tiles:** the game's own marble texture, the grey one I found in your ROM earlier, tinted per screen, so it's still the game's look. It's read from your ROM at run time like everything else.

- **The 9 × 7 bulge:** each tile is its own piece, placed and tilted so the grid curves outward like the game's sphere.

**The animations:**
- **Screen to screen, same colour:** the grid stays exactly as it is.
- **Screen to screen, new colour:** the far background fades to the new colour, and the tiles **flip over in a ripple**, one after another, to show the new colour on their backs.
- **Into a screen without the grid** (starting play, Credits if it has none): the tiles **fly towards you and past the camera**. This doubles as the launch transition, before the loading screen.
- **Back from such a screen:** the tiles **fly in** and settle into the grid.

**Two questions:**
1. **Which colour for which screens?** The game uses blue for the main menu, red for the player pages and green for the mode pages. One idea:
   - **blue:** main menu, Options, Profiles;
   - **green:** Solo, Story and the mode lists;
   - **red:** Local and Versus;
   - or each mode (Story, Hide & Seek, Puzzle, Lines) gets its own colour, which would help people know where they are.
2. **Credits and "Who is playing?":** grid or plain? I'd keep the grid on both, for consistency.

**Size:** it's a medium-to-large piece: the tile renderer, the flip and fly animations, then wiring each screen to its colour. It's self-contained, though. I'd do it in two steps:
1. the grid with colour changes between menus;
2. the fly-in and fly-out, joined up with the loading screen.

Are we basically building a brand new set of menus which launch the game as desired?
If not.. would that be the better way rather than sitting it on top of the old menus?

### Assistant (2026-11-09 16:15)

Yes, mostly. The menus you see and use are already entirely new: every screen, list, hint and setting is BlockPlanet's own, drawn by BlockPlanet. The original menus aren't styled or reused.

**What's still "on top" is how a game gets started.** When you pick a stage, BlockPlanet starts the original game's own menu code *behind* the scenes and presses through it (Single → player page → mode page) to reach the mode. The original menu is still running underneath the whole time, just hidden. That's why we've been chasing its leftovers: the grids, models, sounds, attract demo and odd timing.

**Your instinct is right: launching directly is the better way.** For each mode, BlockPlanet would set up what the old menus would have set (mode, chapter, stage, difficulty, save slot) and call the game's own "start this mode" routine. The old menus would then never run, and:
- no hidden pages, sounds or demo to cover up;
- faster launches;
- the loading screen and grid fly-out become pure presentation, not cover;
- fewer odd states, like that refused launch.

**Why we didn't start that way:** pressing through the old menus is guaranteed to set a mode up exactly as the original does. Launching directly means first learning everything those menus set, mode by mode. Miss one value and you get a subtle bug, like the wrong difficulty or a leftover score from the last game.

**How I'd get there, gradually and safely:**
1. **Research one mode first**, Story: record what the menus set before play starts, then reproduce it and compare both ways.
2. **Switch that mode to direct launch,** keeping the old route as a fallback.
3. **Repeat for each mode:** Training, Puzzle, Hide & Seek, Lines, Versus, Time Trial.
4. **Finally, boot straight into BlockPlanet:** intro → title → Who is playing? → our menus, with the old menu code never reached.

The menus we're building now stay exactly as they are. Only the plumbing underneath changes. It's a good research project for focused sessions with the ROM here. It also feeds the "hold on GAME OVER" work, since that's the same kind of digging.

Shall I add it to the roadmap as a priority, starting with Story?

### Assistant (2026-11-09 16:43)

Yes, I think there's a lot in it. It's how many modern puzzle games are built: **one game engine, plus a "ruleset" that describes each mode as data.** Story, Hide & Seek, Puzzle and Lines then become presets, and new modes (your Custom, Multiphasic, a fast flat-shaded mode, new versus modes) are just new combinations.

**Why it's a good fit here:**
- The modes already differ mostly in **settings**, not fundamentals: layers, block types, the objective, lives, timers, goals, hidden pictures, the friend inside.
- **Local → Custom** on the menu becomes simple: the player edits the ruleset.
- The new computer opponent, the "your turn" Training steps and network play all want one shared, well-understood set of rules.

**How I'd approach it, in stages:**
1. **The catalogue.** For every mode, list what it has, does, and doesn't have, exactly as you said: every variable, with where the game keeps it and what values each mode uses. There's already a start in `docs/research/modes-matrix.md`, and the direct-launch work will turn up most of these values anyway, since that's literally "what does each mode set?".
2. **A ruleset format.** One description per mode, in a data file BlockPlanet reads. The built-in modes get written out as rulesets that reproduce the original exactly.
3. **Apply rulesets to the game's own engine** wherever a variable maps to something the game already supports: lives, timers, layers, block types, objectives, music, background, goals. That alone lets you mix and match quite a lot.
4. **The hard part: playfield shape and size.** The original engine has a fixed board (a 32 × 32 grid per layer, wrapped round a sphere). Other shapes and sizes need BlockPlanet's **own game engine**, the same one the network play and the fast mode notes call for. It's a big job, but it makes everything else open-ended.

**A natural order:** direct launch first, since it produces the per-mode values, then the catalogue, the ruleset format and step 3, with step 4 as a long-term goal.

in terms of our workflow, back and forth etc is our batch file set up in the most logical manor?

### Assistant (2026-11-09 20:06)

Mostly yes. One file, one menu, and a label in the game that tells you where you are covers the essentials. The weak spot is that **every switch rebuilds**, which costs a few minutes each way. Going back and forth to compare a branch with main costs the most.

**Ways it could be better, most useful first:**
1. **Side-by-side builds.** Each branch you try gets its own copy and build folder, so switching becomes instant: Play main, Play menu-grid, compare straight away. The first build of each branch is slow, like your first setup, and each copy takes a few GB of disk. Then later updates only rebuild what changed. Worth it if you'll often compare branches.
2. **A more informative branch list.** Show when each branch was last updated and its latest change, for example `menu-grid · 2 hours ago · pause colours from the original`. Then you know whether there's anything new before switching.
3. **Update on a branch also brings in main's latest.** At the moment a branch only has main's newer fixes if its session merges them in, as I've been asking them to.
4. **"Branch finished" housekeeping.** Once a branch is merged into main, hide it from the list, so it only shows things still being worked on.

My suggestion: **2 and 4** are quick and low-risk. **1** is the big quality-of-life win, if you have the disk space and expect to keep testing branches in parallel, as now with the grid and direct-launch. Which would you like?

Here's what I found about the animated backgrounds behind the sphere, from the game's own code:

- **What they are:** each one is a 3D animated scene, a shape plus a motion file, made with the same kind of animation tool as the title's robots. There are 25 of them, and the game picks one per stage by a rule set for each mode.
- **How they move:** they follow scripts. The motion is stored as keyframes in each background's own file, played and looped by the game's general animation player. No background has its own special code.
- **What we could change, from easiest to hardest:**
  1. **Pick a different one per stage**, from the 25: easy.
  2. **Speed it up or slow it down**, for the background only: easy.
  3. **Recolour or tint it:** fairly easy, since we already recolour the title robots this way.
  4. **Mix and match** shapes and motions from different backgrounds, or bring in other scenes from the game: medium.
  5. **Make completely new ones**, either by writing new animation files in the game's format, or by having BlockPlanet draw its own background, the way it draws the menu tiles: bigger.

### Owner (2026-11-10 18:28)

curious.. what is the format of raw.. is it the same for all n64?

### Assistant (2026-11-10 18:28)

No, there isn't one format for all N64 games. The N64 has no built-in music format: its audio chip mixes whatever sound data the game's own code gives it, so each game picks its own way of storing music.

- **Nintendo's standard kit:** Nintendo supplied a toolkit that many games used. It stores music as compressed MIDI files and the instrument sounds as banks of compressed samples. Tools exist to convert those to normal MIDI.
- **Custom formats:** plenty of developers wrote their own music players instead, for example Rare, Factor 5 with its MusyX system, and Konami. Each needs its own converter.
- **Tetrisphere** is one of the custom ones. Its songs start with the label "DCM1" and look like a tracker module: channels and patterns, like the old Amiga and PC music trackers. That fits its techno soundtrack.

The "raw" files I saved are simply the song's bytes copied straight out of the ROM, unchanged. The converter's job is to read them as the game's player does and write them out as MIDI notes.

- **Track 308, later in the intro, about 5 seconds:** held pad notes, plus an echoed impact that repeats eight times early on, in fading steps. That impact is the most effect-like part.
- **Shared sounds:** the two intro pieces use the same pad and impact sounds. Neither uses any sound from the title music, so the effects are written into the intro's own score, not a separate effects track. That fits your idea.

**Things to know when you open them:**
- Each track is one of the game's voices. The game hands voices out note by note, so a track isn't always one instrument throughout.
- The instruments are the game's own samples, so they won't sound like the game in a normal MIDI player. The track names give the game's sample number for each note.
- Timing is exact. The exact key of each instrument may be off, because the game doesn't record each sample's original note, but the intervals are right.

**The research report on Tetrisphere's music and Neil Voss.** One big limit first: this environment blocks the helpers from opening web pages, so everything comes from search-result snippets. The report marks what's confirmed and what's fan claim. The highlights:
- **How it was made:** Voss wrote everything, music and sound effects, in FastTracker II on a PC, using samples from his own records and sample CDs. "Extol" uses Balinese singers. It played back on H2O's own sound driver, written by programmer David Pridie. That fits what we found: the songs are a recording of a tracker player's output.
- **His background:** born 1974, self-taught on a Commodore 64. He joined H2O when the game was still Phear for the Atari Jaguar.
- **Hidden tunes:** entering the name G[alien head]MEBOY unlocks nine hidden 8-bit style tunes, almost certainly the nine names in the game's track list. The European version swaps "Flim Flam" for "Extol".
- **Releases:** there has never been an official soundtrack, only fan rips. Voss reportedly still has the original tracker files.
- **Reception:** Nintendo Power named it Best Soundtrack of 1997. Today it's a cult favourite.
- **Sequel:** none was ever planned or announced that anyone found, and H2O closed in 2001.

The best sources weren't readable here: the 1998 two-part IGN interview "Composing Tetrisphere" and Nintendojo's interview with Voss. If you want, I can ask you to approve web access for this environment, then re-run the research on the full pages, including those interviews.

### Owner (2026-11-10 20:06)

i'm confused, the sound effects that play.. they are seperate audio files?

### Assistant (2026-11-10 20:07)

Not quite. Two layers are worth separating here.

1. **The samples are separate:** the game has a bank of short recordings: drum hits, pads, booms, whooshes. Each is its own small sound, a bit like separate audio files.
2. **What plays them is a single piece:** the intro's music (track 297) is one score. That score triggers the samples at set times, just as it triggers notes. The intro's "sound effects" (the big hits and the whooshes) are written into that same score, played by the same music player, alongside the pads and arpeggios. They're not a separate track running beside the music.

That's why they always line up: they are the music. It's also why the WAV files I sent could split them, by grouping the score's notes by which sample they play into a music-only file and an effects-only file.

So the fast-forward option moves the effects and the music together, because they're the same piece.

### Assistant (2026-11-10 22:06)

It's still the biggest of the new mode ideas, but it's less problematic than when we wrote it down, because of three things since:
- **BlockPlanet now builds and draws the play sphere itself,** so drawing it from inside (the inner faces, culling flipped) is our own code, not the game's.
- **The brick sky is exactly a sphere of bricks seen from inside,** so we've already tested how that looks and how it can turn.
- **We now know where the sphere's angles and cells are kept,** plus the camera and view matrices from the background work.

What's still hard is the game logic. In Escape you drop blocks onto the underside of the existing blocks, so the drop direction and gravity reverse, and those rules are spread across many of the game's functions. Missed blocks dissolving and costing a life is new logic too.

I'd explore it in two steps, so you can judge it before the hard part:
1. **Visual prototype:** a test switch that puts the camera inside the play sphere looking out, with the game playing as normal. That shows whether play is readable from inside: the board, the pieces, the cursor, the HUD, lighting. It's moderate work and doesn't touch the rules.
2. **Rules research:** find where the game decides drop direction, landing and gravity, and what it would take to reverse them. Report how big that is before building anything.

The menu-grid session is free and knows the sphere drawing and the brick sky best, so I'd give it step 1, with step 2's research alongside. Want me to start it?

One design decision is yours. Under the game's own rule, a piece only counts as supported if something is under it. A piece you throw up against the underside of the shell has nothing under it, so it would just fall back down. Two ways round it:
1. **Touching counts:** a piece is supported if it touches a block above or below it. Pieces stick where you throw them, and if the blocks they're attached to are cleared, they fall towards the core as you described.
2. **Fixed shell:** the shell's blocks never fall, and only pieces you throw can fall. Simpler, but less dynamic.

I'd suggest 1, since it matches your description.

The session checked the game over four ways: as it is now, with the game's own sphere drawing, with the original HUD, and with both. All four look the same:
1. For about 2 seconds, black bricks appear around the sphere and stream out towards the camera.
2. The camera then pushes into the red GAME OVER letters while bricks keep flying past.
3. It fades to black.

So our changes aren't breaking anything. That's simply what the original does, and the bricks never actually settle onto the sphere. The encasing you remember was more of an impression.

Your fifth layer is doable. It's about two days of work, in four steps:
1. **Hold the camera on the sphere** for about 2 seconds before it pushes into GAME OVER. This is the riskiest part, because the routine that moves the camera hasn't been found yet.
2. **Add a real black layer** on top of every column of the board, so it's drawn in the board's own pattern. Small, a couple of hours.
3. **Fly each new brick in** from near the camera to its place, in a sweep, and hide the game's own flying bricks. About a day.
4. **Time it to the game-over sound,** then the red tiles and the panel come in.

Your options:
1. Build it all.
2. A quick version first: the black shell appears layer by layer without flying. About half a day.
3. Leave the original as it is.

I'd suggest the quick version first, so you can see whether the idea feels right before spending the two days.

The likely cause: before each part of the box art grows in, our code removed its drawing commands entirely, including loading its texture. A later draw could then run with no texture loaded and crash. The fix draws those parts at a tiny size instead of removing them, so everything they set up still happens.

### Owner (2026-11-11 18:30)

loading main branch files now
remind me what rt64 does

### Assistant (2026-11-11 18:31)

RT64 is the part that draws the game's graphics on your PC.

- **What the game does:** the original game never draws anything itself. It sends drawing instructions meant for the N64's graphics chip: "draw these triangles, with this texture, in this colour".
- **What RT64 does:** it takes those instructions and draws them with your PC's graphics card instead, using Direct3D 12 or Vulkan on Windows.
- **Why that matters:** because it's doing the drawing fresh on a modern card, it can give you:
  - higher resolutions than the N64's 320 × 240;
  - widescreen and ultrawide;
  - sharper textures and smoother edges;
  - a high frame rate, by filling in extra frames between the game's own.
- **Our menus:** BlockPlanet's menus, panels, coins and menu grid are drawn through RT64 as well, on top of the game's picture.

RT64 is a separate open-source project by Dario. The Zelda PC versions (Zelda64Recomp) use it too. That's why the Windows build log shows the "Verifying exact clean RT64 checkout" step: the build makes sure our copy of RT64 matches the exact version we use.

If there's ever a graphics problem, like a missing shape, a wrong colour or a flicker, the cause is usually somewhere between the game's drawing instructions and RT64.

I've found and fixed the dynamite bug. The fix is committed on main but not pushed, because you're still testing.

**Dynamite never exploding**
- **The cause:** our new HUD hides the original HUD's skull, the icon shown when you lose a life. The game draws that skull in the same spot as the held magic. Our hiding rule skipped anything drawn there while you weren't holding magic. After you fire the dynamite you're no longer holding it, so its flight and sparks were being skipped too. The game waits for those to finish before the explosion, so it waited forever. That's why everything stayed dark.
- **The fix:** from the moment you use a magic until its effects finish, nothing in that spot is hidden.
- **Tested here:** in Story the dynamite now explodes, opens the core, and the level finishes ("Nice Job", then 1:2). I've sent you the screenshots. In Casual it explodes too. The skull still stays hidden when you lose a life normally, and all the automated tests pass.
- **Not just Casual:** this would have affected every magic in Story and Casual, since they're all drawn in the same spot.

**The crash** is intermittent here too. Three of my five runs failed, always as the title's first letter flies in. I've passed everything I found to the launch branch's session, since it's that branch's code. It'll tell you when there's a fix to try.

**Your Casual request** (no lives or countdown, and episodes only open once you've played them in Story) is in the roadmap as low priority. I haven't built it yet.

Keep the notes coming. Say when you're done and I'll push.

### Assistant (2026-11-11 21:10)

The launch branch's session has found a likely cause for the crash.

When the box art appears, our menu layer starts up and loads its pictures and fonts onto the graphics card. It's meant to keep each upload around long enough for the card to finish copying it. During the box art, though, it counts frames twice as fast as normal, so it can throw an upload away while the card is still reading it. That would explain both your crash and the freeze I saw, at that exact moment.

The fix keeps each upload for at least a full second. The session is now testing it with ten runs using a profile, which is the setup that failed before. I'll tell you when it's ready to try.

**How it plays**

  - Small: 9 × 9, 10 mines
  - Medium: 12 × 12, 24 mines
  - Large: 16 × 16, 40 mines

- **The line under the title** shows how many mines are left to flag, or "Cleared!" when you win.

### Assistant (2026-11-11 23:00)

Yes, it's possible, and part of it already exists. RT64, the part that draws the game, has a built-in developer inspector that BlockPlanet simply doesn't switch on at the moment. It includes:

- **A Debugger tab with a free camera:** you can pause a frame and fly the camera around it. That lets you look behind the sphere, the tunnel or the backdrop, which is exactly what you're after.
- **A draw-call list:** every shape the game drew in that frame. You can pick one to see what it is and what texture it used, or hide it.
- **Its renderer settings**, for comparing how things look.

It has **no true wireframe view** (just the outlines of every shape). We could add one as its own drawing mode, but that's more work. The free camera and draw-call list would probably answer "what's back there?" faster anyway.

My suggestion: switch on RT64's inspector as a developer option, only when you start the game with a developer switch, so normal players never see it. It opens as an overlay window over the game, and you could try it on the next build. Want me to do that?

Yes, you're testing on the launch branch (direct-launch). The developer tools are on main for now (commit 930cafc). I've asked the launch branch's session to bring them in with its next update, so they'll arrive when you next choose 3.

**How to use them** (also written up in `docs/DEVELOPER-TOOLS.md`):

1. In BlockPlanet.bat, choose the new option **7 Play with developer tools**.
2. In the game, press **F1**. A "Game editor" window opens over the game. Press F1 again to close it.
3. Open the **Debugger** tab. From there:
   - **Pause or resume:** press **F4**, or the Pause button, to freeze the picture on one frame.
   - **Pick a shape:** right-click on the game to select the shape drawn there. The tab then shows what it is, including its texture and settings. Hovering over a shape in its list lights it up pink on screen.
   - **Free camera:** tick "Free Camera Enabled", then pick a scene, such as the sphere, the tunnel or the intro.
     - **Middle-mouse drag** moves the camera sideways and up and down.
     - **Ctrl + middle-mouse drag** moves it forwards and back.
     - **Alt + middle-mouse drag** turns it, so you can look behind things.

**Good to know:**
- While the window is open, your mouse and keyboard control it, not the game.
- F2 and F3 are taken by the inspector in this mode.
- There's no wireframe view, but the free camera and the highlighted shapes show what's behind things.

I checked on Linux that F1 opens the window. I haven't yet tried the free camera or picking shapes, because the test tools here couldn't click inside that window. So those parts will be your first real test.

### Assistant (2026-11-11 23:47)

Glad the flat version plays well. And yes, 32 × 32 is the natural size: it's the size of the game's board. It also wraps round in both directions, so every cell has eight neighbours and there are no edges or corners. The rules I wrote already support wrapping.

**Your design, as I understand it:**
- **Start:** one layer of blue cubes over a dark grey core divided by black lines. The cubes could be chrome, which the N64 loved.
- **Uncover:** the drop button removes the cube under the cursor, with an animation still to decide. Underneath is either a number on the core or a mine. A mine flashes and explodes, with the effect to decide later.
- **Flag:** the slide button.
- **Win:** the mines are revealed in green. The sphere spins twice to show where they all were, then fades out.
- **Lose:** the same, but the remaining cubes fade away and the mines show red. Later this gets the black closing blocks and a Game Over screen.

**How I'd build it:** run it inside a real game stage, like the test stages, but with our own board.
- **The cubes:** each frame BlockPlanet writes the board, so the outer layer is all blue bricks and the core sits underneath. The game then draws the sphere, turns it and moves the cursor exactly as in play.
- **Your buttons:** drop and slide are caught before the game acts on them, and become "uncover" and "flag".
- **Numbers and mines:** drawn by BlockPlanet on top of the core cells, the same way we already place pop-ups over the sphere.
- **The win and lose spins:** the camera spins we already know how to drive.

**Two things to decide first:**

1. **How many mines?** 1,024 cells is a lot. Classic difficulty would be about 150 to 200 mines, which makes a long game. Options:
   - an Easy/Medium/Hard choice, such as 80, 130 or 180 mines;
   - a smaller field, using only part of the sphere, though then it wouldn't wrap all the way round.
2. **A safe start?** Like the flat version, the first cube you uncover would never be a mine. Keep that?

Once you answer, I'll write this into the roadmap and start on the first piece: a test stage with the all-blue sphere, where uncovering a cube shows its number.

### Owner (2026-11-12 14:53)

Any idea how you’ll get the numbers on the texture etc?

### Assistant (2026-11-12 14:53)

Yes. I'd have BlockPlanet draw the numbers itself, as small 3D tiles laid on the core.

**How it would work**
1. **Our own digit art.** A small sheet of digits 1 to 8, plus a flag and a mine, in the same style as the flat Minefield's numbers. A script would draw it, the way the coins are made, so it's our art and can go in the project.
2. **Loaded into the game's spare memory.** When the minefield starts, BlockPlanet puts the digit sheet into the free upper 4 MB, where it already keeps the cube texture table. The graphics layer can then use it like any of the game's own textures.
3. **Corner positions from the face drawing.** The core's faces already go through BlockPlanet's face drawing, so as each core cell is drawn we know its four corners on the sphere.
4. **A digit tile on top.** For each uncovered cell with a number, BlockPlanet adds one more square at those corners, lifted a hair above the core, textured with that digit and see-through round it.
5. **Drawn after the core pass.** All the digit tiles are drawn in one batch after the core pass finishes, so the game's own core drawing isn't disturbed.

**Why this is better than the floating numbers**
- **Part of the sphere:** the digits turn, zoom and tilt with it, shrinking towards the edges as real tiles would.
- **Hidden properly:** cubes in front cover them.
- **No more drifting:** they can't sit off the edge or slip out of place as the camera moves.
- **Reusable:** the same method could show mines, flags and other marks, for this mode and others.

**The tricky part** is the graphics commands for loading our texture and blending it in. It's similar to what BlockPlanet already does for the title's ring, so I'd reuse that code.

**There's another route:** a replacement texture pack, swapping the core's tile pictures for ones with digits. That's simpler to draw, but it would also change the cores in Puzzle and other modes, so I'd avoid it.

### Owner (2026-11-12 19:01)

mad question.. if we combined two recomps.. you e potentially use stages from that other game as backgrounds fo tetrisphere? if i owned both games

### Assistant (2026-11-12 19:01)

Not mad at all, and it's possible as long as you own both games. The same rule we follow now would apply: nothing from either game gets committed. BlockPlanet would read your own copy of the other game at install time, just as it reads Tetrisphere today.

What doesn't work well is actually combining the two recomps. Both games expect to own the whole N64: the same memory, the same graphics state, the same timing. Running both in one program would mean separating everything they share, which is a project on its own.

There are three easier ways:

1. **Pull out the stage art when installing.** A converter reads the other game's stage models and textures from your copy. BlockPlanet then draws them behind the sphere, much like the tunnel backdrop now. This is the best result, because the backgrounds are real 3D and the camera can move through them. It depends on how well the other game's file formats are understood: easy if someone has already taken that game apart (some N64 games are fully documented), hard if not.
2. **Pre-render the backgrounds.** Play through the other game's stages once at install time, record looping clips or panoramas, and use those as backdrops. It works for any game, but the backgrounds are flat images rather than real 3D.
3. **Run the other game alongside, invisibly.** Run it in the background and use its live picture as the backdrop. It's the most impressive, but it's heavy on the computer and fiddly to keep stable.

Which game did you have in mind? That decides whether option 1 is realistic. If its stage files are already understood, it's quite doable. Either way, it would go on the roadmap rather than being started now.

are we drawing the numbers on the core the same way that pictures are hidden on the core in hide and seek? .. those pictures stay when the board spins

### Assistant (2026-11-12 19:21)

No, they're drawn differently, and your question points at the better way.

**How it works now:** the game draws the sphere, and afterwards BlockPlanet draws the numbers on top as separate little squares. I have to work out each square's position myself, and once the board scrolls I get it wrong.

**How Hide & Seek does it:** the picture is part of the core itself. Each core square holds a value, and the game draws that square from the matching piece of a texture. Values 72–80 are the nine pieces of a 3×3 picture. The game places those squares itself, so they stay put whatever the board does.

**Doing the numbers the same way:** we'd stop drawing on top, and instead:
1. Make a 3×3 picture sheet of our own: the digits 1–8, plus a blank piece for squares with no number.
2. When Minefield is running, put our sheet in memory wherever the game reads the Hide & Seek picture from.
3. Give each opened core square the value of the piece it needs (72 + the number), and plain core values elsewhere.

The game then draws the numbers as part of the core, so they turn with the sphere and can't drift. That also lets me remove the separate drawing pass and the scroll problem along with it.

The one thing to find out is where the game loads the picture texture from, and in what format, so our sheet can stand in for it. That's research, but the picture values themselves already work in Minefield. We saw 72–80 showing picture tiles when we tested core values.

I think this is the right fix for the drifting numbers. Shall I switch to it now, before the window size and position change?

That error usually just means the game is still open. Windows won't let the build replace `tetrisphere-m1.exe` while it's running, so the link step can't write the new file.

1. Close the game if it's open. If you can't see a window, open Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc), find **tetrisphere-m1.exe** and choose **End task**. A crashed or half-closed copy sometimes lingers there.
2. Run option 3 in `BlockPlanet.bat` again. The build picks up where it stopped.

If it still fails with nothing running, your antivirus may be scanning the new file. Waiting a few seconds and running option 3 again normally gets past that.

**Difficulty:** I wrote a solver that plays each arena hundreds of times. It sees only the numbers and its own flags, never the mines, makes every certain move, and guesses only when it must. Win rates, as a cautious estimate for a careful player:

| Arena | Won at today's mine counts |
| --- | ---: |
| Full | 96% |
| Horizon | 94% |
| Half | 93% |
| Crossover | 92% |
| Mini | 90% |
| Bow | 88% |
| Decompartmental | 29% |

- **Today's mine counts are easy.** They're about 12.7% of the cells, roughly the classic game's beginner level.
- **Difficulty depends mostly on the share of cells that hide mines,** and it changes fast. At 17.5% most arenas drop to 60–90%, and at 20% to 35–80%. That would make natural levels later: easy 12.5%, medium 15%, hard 17.5%, expert 20%.
- **The whole sphere is the easiest shape at any mine count,** because it has no edges or corners to guess in.
- **Decompartmental is the luck arena,** as you said: every compartment starts with a blind guess.

The full tables are in `docs/research/minefield-difficulty.md`. Lower cubes and the win and lose endings are on the roadmap.

### Owner (2026-11-13 16:14)

q - how possible would it be to scale this game down and package for SNES and Super FX Chip2?

### Assistant (2026-11-13 16:14)

It's possible as a new game written for the SNES, but not as a scaled-down port of BlockPlanet. A rough picture:

**Why it can't be a port**
- **No shared code:** BlockPlanet works by running the original N64 game's own code, translated for PC. None of that can go to a SNES; it's a different processor and a far smaller machine (about 1/20th of the N64's memory and speed). A SNES version would be written from scratch.
- **Rights:** Tetrisphere itself (its name, look and levels) belongs to Nintendo and the original developers, so a SNES "Tetrisphere" isn't something to make. An original game in the same spirit is fine, and Minefield on the sphere is already BlockPlanet's own design, so it's the natural candidate.

**What the Super FX 2 could manage**
- **The chip:** it's a 21 MHz graphics chip that draws flat-shaded polygons into a smaller window, like Star Fox 2 and Doom on the SNES. Expect a low resolution (about 224×160 or less), maybe 15–20 frames a second, and a few hundred simple polygons a frame.
- **The sphere:** about 15×15 visible cells of cubes, around 300–600 faces, is right at that limit, with flat colours instead of textures. It's doable for a simplified sphere: flat cubes, no fancy lighting.
- **Pre-drawn sprites instead:** a cheaper trick is to pre-draw the sphere at each turn angle as sprites. It's less flexible, but it runs without the Super FX at all.
- **The rest suits the SNES well:** Minefield's logic, menus and the numbers on the core.

**Effort and practicalities**
- **Effort:** months of work in 65816 assembly plus Super FX code, with SNES homebrew tools. Running it in an emulator (bsnes, Mesen) is easy.
- **Real hardware:** Super FX carts need donor boards or a flash cart that supports the chip (the FXPak Pro does).

If you want to explore it, a sensible first step would be a small proof of concept in an emulator: a flat-shaded rotating sphere of cubes with the Minefield rules. That would show quickly whether the frame rate feels acceptable. It would be its own project, separate from BlockPlanet. Want me to put it on the roadmap as an idea for later?

### Assistant (2026-11-13 16:25)

I've added it to the roadmap on `main` as an idea for later: "A SNES version of Minefield on the sphere, with the Super FX 2". It covers:
- **Why it's a new game:** it would be written from scratch, not a port of BlockPlanet.
- **What the chip can manage:** a flat-shaded sphere at a low resolution and frame rate, with pre-drawn sprites as a fallback.
- **First step:** a small proof of concept in an emulator.
- **Effort:** months of work, and a Super FX board or a compatible flash cart to run it on real hardware.

It's only a document change, so there's no need to rebuild for it.

- **Plugging the PC in:** the simplest route, and BlockPlanet already plays well on a big screen. The menus are designed for a TV and a controller, and the HUD keeps clear of the edges.

### Assistant (2026-11-14 19:57)

That TV makes the answer clearer. The UE75TU7020 is Samsung's 2020 budget 4K model, on Tizen 5.5 with a fairly modest quad-core chip.

**Running BlockPlanet on the TV itself: not realistic.** Tizen apps from outside developers are web apps, written in HTML and JavaScript or WebAssembly, and they get only basic browser graphics. They have no access to the Vulkan or Direct3D that BlockPlanet's renderer relies on. Even rebuilt from scratch for the web, the TV's chip would struggle to run an N64 game translated to PC plus our extras at a steady speed. I'd rule this one out.

**Streaming from your PC: the way to go.** The PC does the work and the TV only shows the picture and passes on the controller.
1. **Steam Link:** Valve made a Steam Link app for Samsung TVs from 2016 on, so it should be in your TV's app store. Search for "Steam Link". Then add BlockPlanet to Steam on the PC as a non-Steam game and start it from the TV. Whether the app is still offered for 2020 models is something I can't check from here.
2. **Moonlight:** if Steam Link isn't there, Moonlight is an open-source alternative that streams from the PC through Sunshine. It isn't in Samsung's store, but there's a community Tizen build you can install with the TV in developer mode. It takes about an hour to set up, and you've already done Tizen development for CurioCat.
3. **An HDMI cable:** the simplest of all, if the PC can sit near the TV.

On your network, 4K streaming at 60 frames a second needs a wired connection, or very good Wi-Fi, for the PC at least. Bluetooth controllers can pair with the TV, though a controller plugged into the PC is often more reliable.

If streaming works out, I can add a "TV" choice to `BlockPlanet.bat` that starts the game fullscreen at 4K and sized for a 75-inch screen. Want me to?

### Assistant (2026-11-14 20:02)

Yes, that's the same arrangement as the PC version, and it could work the same way. The app ships with nothing from the game. It reads your own ROM backup from the USB drive the first time it starts and builds what it needs from that. Nothing from the game is ever in the app itself.

There are two ways to use the ROM, and only one suits the TV:

1. **Run the real game code: no.** On PC, the ROM's code is translated ahead of time into PC code and then compiled, which takes a PC's toolchain and many minutes. A TV app can't do that. The alternative is emulating the N64 in the browser (WebAssembly emulators exist), but your TV's chip is far too slow to emulate an N64 smoothly, and emulation is the part we deliberately avoid.
2. **Use the ROM for its art and sound, with our own simple game code: yes.** The app would take the brick textures, colours, the core and maybe the music from your ROM, and play our own casual rules on a simplified sphere. That fits the TV idea well: it looks and sounds like Tetrisphere, while the game logic is ours, and BlockPlanet's research already knows where much of that art lives in the ROM.

Two practical checks before relying on it:
- **USB access:** Tizen web apps need a permission to read USB storage, and Samsung's 2020 TVs may restrict it for apps that aren't from partners. The first test page should check that along with the graphics speed.
- **Distribution:** an app that turns a Tetrisphere ROM into Tetrisphere-looking play shouldn't go on Samsung's app store under that name. Installing it on your own TV in developer mode, as with CurioCat while testing, is fine. Anything for the store would have to stand on its own art.

Shall I add this to the TV entry on the roadmap: art and sound from the player's own ROM on the USB drive, our own game code, and the two checks?

The mouse now works in play, and Escape pauses. Option 3 in the batch file picks it up.

**How it plays:**
- **Hold the left button and drag:** turns the sphere in any direction, diagonals included. The sphere follows your hand. Moving the pointer about a twelfth of the window's height moves one cell.
- **Left click without dragging:** drops the piece where the cursor is.
- **Hold the right button:** slides the piece. Drag while holding to move it the way the pointer goes.
- **Wheel:** moves up and down one cell per notch. A horizontal wheel moves left and right.
- **Middle button:** fires the magic.
- **Escape:** pauses in play, the same as Enter. In menus it still goes back.

**Tested so far:** in a Rescue stage, dragging turned the sphere, the wheel moved the cursor, a click dropped a piece (it scored a combo), and Escape opened the pause screen. I haven't tried the right-button slide, the middle button or the horizontal wheel in the game yet. Their automated tests pass, but please try them on your PC. If turning feels too slow or fast, or goes the opposite way to what you expect, tell me and I'll change it.

When a "how to play" card is too long to fit, the wheel scrolls the card instead of moving the cursor.

**How it works:** a Hide & Seek episode is 30 levels, and the game has no Continue/Exit menu of its own. After level 30 it plays its rescue scene, then shows the "Congratulations, you finished the first episode…" card. BlockPlanet's panel now comes up before that card, the same as Rescue's:

**Fixes found along the way:**
- **Level 30's best time was never saved,** because the level number goes back to 1 rather than on to 31.
- **Level best times were all stored as one episode.** They're now kept per episode, and your existing bests count as Episode 1's.
- **The intro skip could close a goal card before you saw it.** It now presses A once, plus one retry 2.5 seconds later only if needed, instead of repeatedly.

So when the last heart goes, the piece already exists. It's that landed (or still settling) piece that pokes out above the shell, because the board never accepted it as part of the sphere.

You're right that the cleaner fix would be for the game to check before launching. But that changes how a drop plays: the miss would be decided before you see the piece fall, and the original lets you watch it land and fail. That runs against your rule that every mode plays as the original, so I'd go with hiding it. While the shell is up, BlockPlanet would skip drawing the dropped piece, the same way it now hides the piece's shadow.

To do that I first need to find which part of the game draws the falling piece. I can do that next, along with the dark bricks in the game's own sequence, since both are draw-skips in the same area.

### Assistant (2026-11-17 00:23)

The jukebox is now a Winamp-style player, and it's pushed to both branches. To try it, update with BlockPlanet.bat option 3, then pick the music icon on the main menu.

**What's on the player**
- **Display:** a large clock showing how long the track has played, the track number and name, "Track 7 of 23 · Playing", a 16-bar spectrum that moves with the music, and a line showing the current shuffle, repeat and background settings.
- **Buttons:** Previous, Play, Stop, Next, Shuffle, Repeat, Playlist and Background. Shuffle and Repeat light up when they're on.
- **Volume:** a music volume slider, the same setting as the Audio page, so changes are saved.
- **Playlist:** opens all 23 tracks; choosing one plays it.

**Backgrounds that react to the music** (the Background button cycles through them):
- **Pulse:** the whole grid lifts and brightens with the beat.
- **Bars:** columns of the grid light up by pitch, bass on the left.
- **Water:** the normal grid.

**Things that don't work quite like Winamp yet**
- **Stop is really a mute.** The game's song keeps running underneath, and Play starts the track again from the beginning. A true Pause that resumes mid-song would need me to find how to pause the game's song player.
- **Repeat off is approximate.** The game's tracks loop forever, so Repeat on (the default) is the game's normal behaviour. The game gives no track lengths, so with Repeat off it moves to the next track after three minutes.
- **The clock shows "-:--" at first.** The game's menu music didn't start from the jukebox, so its time is unknown. The clock starts once you play a track.
- **Settings aren't saved.** Shuffle, Repeat and the background choice reset each session for now.
- **The panel hides most of the background.** The movement is easiest to see around the edges.

I've noted these in the roadmap, along with a way to hide the player and just watch the background, and more backgrounds.

Tracks 15 to 23 now play, the jukebox has three new Winamp-style backgrounds and a hide button, and I've written up what's still missing. Everything is pushed to both branches and the 81 tests pass. Update with option 3 in the morning.

**Why the last tracks didn't play**
Those nine tracks (Magic Fluter to Birthday Bumps) are the game's hidden bonus music. The game won't start any track past the 14th unless you've entered the "G + alien + MEBOY" name code. The jukebox now lifts that limit only when it starts a track, so all 23 play. The pause menu's track choice works for them too. The game's own Auto and Random music is unchanged, so the bonus tracks still don't come up there. In the test run, the game's music player loaded tracks 14 to 23 as soon as they were chosen.

**New backgrounds**
The tiles are still the default (Pulse). The Background button now cycles through three more, built from the game's marble brick texture:
- **Spectrum:** a wall of bricks like Winamp's classic analyser, lit from the bottom in blue, teal, yellow, orange and red. White peak bricks fall back slowly.
- **Scope:** the sound wave traced in small bricks, with a fainter trace of the previous moment behind it.
- **Pieces:** coloured pieces drop through the dark, a new one on each beat, falling faster when the music is loud.

There's also a new eye button next to Back that hides the player so you can just watch. Any button or click brings it back.

**What's still missing** (written up in `docs/research/jukebox.md`)
- **A real Pause:** it would need the game's song player held still. I haven't researched how yet.
- **Track lengths:** these would give a "time left" display, a seek bar, and Repeat-off moving on at the real end of a track. The lengths could come from each song's loop point.
- **Easy additions:** balance, an equaliser, keyboard media keys, and remembering your shuffle, repeat and background choices.
- **Bigger items:** crossfade between tracks, skins, and the sound test.

**Using the game's 3D models**
The game draws its own models, so I can't simply place them in the menus. Three ways that could work, cheapest first:
1. Find what the VORTEX name code plays. It's an animation, so it might be a ready-made visualiser.
